title: Container Security: Scanning, Signing & Least Privilege
summary: Hardens container images from build to runtime: layer-aware image design, vulnerability scanning, image signing, non-root execution, read-only filesystems, and why secrets never belong in environment variables.
objectives: Explain how Dockerfile layers accumulate and why deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image
Scan container images for known vulnerabilities and act on high-severity findings before shipping
Run containers as non-root users with read-only root filesystems and justify each control
Explain why storing secrets in environment variables is an antipattern and describe safer alternatives
Describe distroless images and SBOMs and how signing proves an image came from your pipeline

notes.title: Layers Are Immutable History
notes.body: Every Dockerfile instruction that touches the filesystem (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new layer, and layers are stacked immutably — a later layer can hide a file but never erases the bytes of an earlier one. Worked example: a Dockerfile starts FROM a 60 MB base image, runs apt-get install adding 180 MB of packages, then a later RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists removes 40 MB of package lists. A learner guessing the final size might say 60 + 180 - 40 = 200 MB. The correct answer is about 240 MB: the deletion creates a tiny new layer containing only whiteout markers (metadata saying 'these files are hidden'), while the original 40 MB of lists still sits in the earlier layer, downloadable by anyone who pulls the image. Solution: never rely on cleanup in later layers — chain install and cleanup in a single RUN (apt-get install && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists) so the lists never land in their own layer, or better, use multi-stage builds so build tools never ship at all.

notes.title: Replacing the Cleanup Step: Does the Size Change?
notes.body: This is a real panel question, so learn to answer it cold. Take the Dockerfile above and replace the final RUN rm -rf ... cleanup step with RUN echo hello. Does the image size change? Worked example: before the change, the image had layers [base 60 MB][packages 180 MB][whiteout cleanup ~1 KB]. After replacing cleanup with echo hello, the layers are [base 60 MB][packages 180 MB][echo ~1 KB]. Solution: yes, the size changes — it gets slightly LARGER, not smaller. The echo layer adds its own few bytes, and more importantly the 40 MB of package lists are no longer hidden, so the effective image now carries them visibly. The deeper lesson the panel wants: layer count and layer content both matter, and 'cleanup' that happens in a separate layer is security theater for size — the deleted data is still in the image and still scannable by an attacker who pulls it.

notes.title: Scan Before You Ship
notes.body: Image scanning compares every package in every layer against vulnerability databases and reports CVEs with severities (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW). Worked example: you build myapp:1.4 FROM python:3.11-slim and run trivy image myapp:1.4. The report shows HIGH CVE-2023-XXXXX in libssl 1.1.1w — a buffer overflow reachable over the network — plus 12 MEDIUMs in unused system packages. Solution path: first check whether a patched base tag exists (python:3.11-slim is rebuilt regularly), rebuild, and re-scan until the HIGH is gone; for the MEDIUMs in packages your app never uses, the durable fix is a slimmer base or multi-stage build that drops them entirely. Operationalize this as a pipeline gate: fail the build on any CRITICAL, and fail on HIGH unless an explicit, time-boxed exception is recorded with an owner. Scanning once is not enough — rescan on a schedule, because new CVEs are published against old images every day.

notes.title: Run as Non-Root
notes.body: Containers run as root by default, which means a process escape or a exploited application bug hands the attacker root inside the container — and a much easier path to the host. Least privilege means the container's processes run as an unprivileged user. Worked example: your Node.js app writes access logs to /var/log/app.log. You add USER appuser to the Dockerfile, rebuild, and the container crashes with EACCES permission denied. Solution: the directory is root-owned in the image. Fix it at build time (RUN mkdir -p /var/log && chown appuser:appuser /var/log) or, in Kubernetes, mount a writable emptyDir volume at /var/log so logs land on an ephemeral volume the user owns. Defense in depth pairs this with a Kubernetes securityContext (runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false) so the platform refuses to start any pod that tries to run as root, catching the misconfiguration before it reaches production.

notes.title: Read-Only Root Filesystem
notes.body: A read-only root filesystem makes the container's entire image layer immutable at runtime: malware cannot drop binaries, attackers cannot modify config, and compromised processes cannot persist. Worked example: you launch your hardened image with docker run --read-only myapp:2.0 and the app immediately crashes writing a temp upload to /tmp/cache.dat. Solution: the app needs designated writable space, not a writable everything. Mount a tmpfs at /tmp (docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp) so temporary files live in memory and vanish with the container, and mount a real volume only where durable writes are required. In Kubernetes the same control is securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true plus explicit volumeMounts. This pairs with non-root: even if an attacker gets code execution, they land in a container where they are not root and cannot write anywhere except the scratch paths you chose.

notes.title: Secrets Do Not Belong in Environment Variables
notes.body: Passing secrets via -e DB_PASSWORD=... or env: in a pod spec feels convenient and is a genuine antipattern: environment variables are visible in docker inspect output, in /proc/<pid>/environ of every process, in Kubernetes API objects readable by anyone with pod-get permission, and they leak into crash dumps and logging agents that capture the environment. Worked example: a developer runs docker inspect on a running container to debug networking and the full production database password scrolls past in the Env array — now it sits in their shell history and terminal scrollback too. Solution: mount secrets as files (Kubernetes Secret volumes land at /var/run/secrets/...), so the application reads the credential from a file that only its user can read, and the value never appears in inspect output or the process environment. For rotation and audit, prefer a secret manager (Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) with the platform injecting short-lived credentials, so a leaked value expires instead of living forever.

notes.title: Distroless Images and SBOMs
notes.body: A distroless image contains your application and its runtime dependencies but no shell, no package manager, and no utilities — there is literally no /bin/sh for an attacker to invoke. Worked example: your Go service built FROM golang:1.22 ships a 900 MB image including a full Debian userland; rebuilt as a multi-stage Dockerfile that copies only the compiled static binary into gcr.io/distroless/static, the final image is ~25 MB and a trivy scan drops from 40 findings to zero, because there are no OS packages left to be vulnerable. The tradeoff: debugging is harder (no shell to exec into), so keep a debug tag with busybox for troubleshooting and ship distroless to prod. An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is the ingredient list of that image — every package and version, generated by tools like syft at build time. Pair the SBOM with signing (cosign sign) and attestation so downstream consumers can verify the image was built by your pipeline and matches the SBOM you published.

notes.title: Signing: Proving the Image Came From Your Pipeline
notes.body: Scanning tells you an image is clean; signing tells you the image is YOURS — that the bits deployed are exactly the bits your pipeline built, not a lookalike pushed by an attacker who compromised a registry credential. Worked example: your pipeline builds myapp:2.0, runs trivy (clean), then runs cosign sign --key azurekms://... myapp:2.0, publishing a signature to the registry. An attacker with stolen push credentials pushes a backdoored myapp:2.0 with the same tag. Solution: your cluster's admission policy verifies the cosign signature before admitting any pod — the attacker's image has no valid signature, so the deployment is rejected and an alert fires. The workflow to internalize: build once, scan, sign, then verify at deploy time. Unsigned images never reach production, and tag mutability stops mattering because the signature pins the exact digest. This closes the loop the earlier notes opened: minimal layers, no secrets, non-root, read-only, scanned, and now provably authentic.

cards.front: Each Dockerfile RUN/COPY/ADD instruction creates what, and can a later layer erase an earlier layer's bytes?
cards.back: A new immutable layer. No — a later layer can only hide files with whiteout markers; the original bytes remain in the earlier layer and ship in the image.

cards.front: You replace a RUN rm -rf cleanup step with RUN echo hello. Does the image get smaller, larger, or stay the same?
cards.back: Slightly larger — the echo adds its own layer, and the files the cleanup was hiding are no longer hidden.

cards.front: What does 'whiteout' mean in container image layers?
cards.back: A marker file in an upper layer that hides a file from a lower layer at runtime, without deleting the lower layer's data.

cards.front: Name the tool/command to scan an image for CVEs, and the two severity levels that should gate a pipeline.
cards.back: trivy image <name:tag> (or equivalent scanner). Fail the build on CRITICAL, and on HIGH unless a time-boxed exception with an owner is recorded.

cards.front: Why run containers as a non-root user?
cards.back: A container escape or app exploit as root gives the attacker root inside the container and an easier path to the host. Non-root contains the blast radius.

cards.front: A container crashes with EACCES after you add USER appuser. What is the fix?
cards.back: chown the writable directories to the user at build time, or mount a writable volume (e.g. emptyDir) at the path the app needs to write.

cards.front: What does a read-only root filesystem prevent, and where do temp files go instead?
cards.back: It prevents any writes to the image layers — no dropped binaries, no modified config, no persistence. Temp files go to an explicit tmpfs mount or a mounted volume.

cards.front: Give three places a secret in an environment variable leaks.
cards.back: docker inspect output, /proc/<pid>/environ, Kubernetes pod specs visible via the API, plus shell history, crash dumps, and log agents that capture the environment (any three).

cards.front: What is the safer alternative to secrets in environment variables?
cards.back: Mount secrets as files (e.g. Kubernetes Secret volumes), or inject short-lived credentials from a secret manager like Vault/Key Vault.

cards.front: What is a distroless image and what is its main tradeoff?
cards.back: An image with only the app and its runtime deps — no shell, no package manager — drastically shrinking attack surface. Tradeoff: harder to debug (no shell to exec into); keep a debug variant.

cards.front: What is an SBOM and when is it generated?
cards.back: A Software Bill of Materials: the complete ingredient list of packages/versions in the image, generated at build time (e.g. with syft).

cards.front: What does image signing with cosign prove, and where is it enforced?
cards.back: It proves the image digest was produced by your pipeline. Enforced at deploy time by admission policy that rejects unsigned images.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile has FROM (60 MB), RUN apt-get install (adds 180 MB), RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists (removes 40 MB). What is the approximate final image size?
choices: About 200 MB — the rm subtracts from the total
About 240 MB — the rm only hides files with whiteout markers
About 60 MB — only the base layer counts
About 180 MB — the base is replaced by the install layer
quiz.explain: Layers are immutable: the rm creates a tiny layer of whiteout markers, but the 180 MB of package data (including the 40 MB of lists) remains in the earlier layer. 60 + 180 ≈ 240 MB.

quiz.q: You replace the cleanup RUN rm -rf step with RUN echo hello. What happens to image size?
choices: It shrinks, because echo is smaller than rm
It stays identical — one RUN replaced another
It grows slightly — the echo adds a layer and the previously hidden files are visible again
It shrinks to just the base plus echo
quiz.explain: The echo layer adds bytes, and without the whiteout markers the 40 MB of package lists are no longer hidden — the image carries more, not less.

quiz.q: trivy image myapp:1.4 reports a HIGH CVE in libssl reachable over the network. What is the correct first response?
choices: Suppress it — the app doesn't call libssl directly
Rebuild from a patched base image tag and re-scan until the HIGH is resolved
Delete the trivy report so the pipeline passes
Switch the scanner to a different tool and hope it doesn't report it
quiz.explain: A network-reachable HIGH in a crypto library is exactly what the gate exists for: rebuild on a patched base, re-scan, and only ship when clean (or with a documented, time-boxed exception).

quiz.q: After adding USER appuser, the container crashes with EACCES writing to /var/log/app.log. Best fix?
choices: Run the container as root again
chmod 777 /var/log in the Dockerfile
chown the log directory to appuser at build time or mount a writable volume there
Write logs to stdout instead of fixing permissions
quiz.explain: The directory is root-owned in the image. Give the non-root user ownership at build time or mount a volume it owns — preserving least privilege instead of reverting to root.

quiz.q: Why is DB_PASSWORD in an environment variable an antipattern? (strongest reason)
choices: Environment variables are slower than files
The value is exposed via docker inspect, /proc/<pid>/environ, and the K8s API to anyone with read access
Files cannot be mounted in containers
Environment variables have a 1 KB size limit
quiz.explain: Env vars are visible in inspect output, every process's /proc environ, and pod specs — they leak into shell history, dumps, and logs. Mounted secret files are readable only by the app's user.

quiz.q: A container launched with --read-only crashes writing a temp file to /tmp. Correct fix?
choices: Remove --read-only
Add --tmpfs /tmp so temp files live in memory
Run as root so it can write anywhere
Set the TMPDIR env var to /proc
quiz.explain: Keep the root filesystem read-only and give the app designated writable scratch space via tmpfs — least privilege preserved, temp files vanish with the container.

quiz.q: What is the primary security benefit of a distroless image?
choices: It runs faster because it has fewer layers
No shell, package manager, or utilities exist for an attacker to use — minimal attack surface
It automatically scans itself for CVEs
It encrypts the application binary
quiz.explain: Distroless strips the entire OS userland; with no shell or tools present, post-exploitation options collapse and there are no OS packages left to carry CVEs.

quiz.q: Your pipeline signs images with cosign. An attacker pushes a backdoored image under the same tag. What stops it reaching production?
choices: Nothing — the tag matches so it deploys
Admission policy verifying the cosign signature rejects the unsigned digest
trivy automatically deletes unsigned images
The registry overwrites it with the old image
quiz.explain: The signature pins the exact digest your pipeline built. The attacker's image lacks a valid signature, so signature-verifying admission control rejects the deployment.

quiz.q: When should an SBOM be generated and what is it for?
choices: At deploy time, to speed up pod startup
At build time, as the complete package/versions inventory enabling vulnerability tracking and provenance
Only after a breach, for forensics
Never — SBOMs are only for open-source licensing
quiz.explain: Generate the SBOM at build time with the image; it lets you answer 'which of my images contain package X at version Y?' the moment a new CVE drops.

items.prompt: Dockerfile: FROM ubuntu (70 MB) / RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl (adds 90 MB) / RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists (frees 30 MB of lists). Final size?
items.answer: ≈160 MB (70 + 90). The rm only adds whiteout markers; the 30 MB of lists remain in the earlier layer.
items.explain: Same-layer cleanup works; cross-layer cleanup does not. Here install and cleanup are separate RUNs, so nothing is reclaimed.

items.prompt: Same Dockerfile, but install and cleanup are chained in ONE RUN with &&. Final size?
items.answer: ≈130 MB (70 + 90 − 30). The lists never land in their own layer, so the single layer only contains the net result.
items.explain: Chaining with && keeps the filesystem delta of one layer equal to the net change — the only reliable in-Dockerfile cleanup.

items.prompt: You COPY a 500 MB dataset into the image, then in the next layer RUN rm the file. An attacker pulls the image. Can they recover the dataset?
items.answer: Yes — the 500 MB still sits in the earlier layer; anyone who pulls the image can extract it.
items.explain: Whiteout hides from the running container's view, not from the image's layer tarballs. Never bake secrets or sensitive data into any layer.

items.prompt: Multi-stage: stage 1 (golang:1.22, 900 MB) compiles a 20 MB static binary; stage 2 (distroless/static) COPY --from=0 only the binary. Final image size?
items.answer: ≈25 MB. Only the final stage's layers ship; the 900 MB build stage is discarded.
items.explain: Multi-stage builds are the structural fix: build tools, caches, and intermediate files never enter the shipped layers at all.

items.prompt: docker history shows 12 layers for a simple web app image. Name two concrete changes that cut layer count AND size.
items.answer: Chain related RUN commands with && (fewer layers), and switch to multi-stage + minimal/distroless base (smaller layers).
items.explain: Fewer layers reduce metadata overhead and accidental duplication; a minimal base removes entire package trees you never needed.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Replacing the cleanup step with RUN echo hello — does the image size change?' Give the one-sentence answer.
items.answer: Yes — it grows slightly, because the echo adds its own layer and the files the cleanup was hiding are no longer hidden.
items.explain: The panel is testing whether you know layers are additive and cleanup-via-later-layer is whiteout-only.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Does removing files in a later layer reduce the image size?' Give the one-sentence answer.
items.answer: No — it adds a whiteout layer while the deleted bytes remain in the earlier layer, so the image stays the same size (or grows by the marker layer).
items.explain: This is the whiteout concept in one line: hiding is not deleting.

items.prompt: A deployment YAML has no securityContext and the image has no USER. Name the three fields to add.
items.answer: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: <uid>, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (plus allowPrivilegeEscalation: false).
items.explain: These four are the standard least-privilege baseline; runAsNonRoot makes the platform reject root execution outright.

items.prompt: The app needs to write uploads durably. With a read-only root filesystem, where do uploads go?
items.answer: A mounted persistent volume (or emptyDir for ephemeral) at the upload path — never by making the root writable.
items.explain: Read-only root plus explicit writable mounts is the pattern: deny-by-default, allow-list the write paths.

items.prompt: A teammate passes an API key via env in the pod spec 'because Secrets are base64 anyway'. What's wrong with this reasoning?
items.answer: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — and env vars additionally leak via inspect, /proc, API reads, history, and dumps. Mounted secret files avoid the env exposure entirely.
items.explain: Two separate issues: Secrets aren't encrypted by default (that's what encryption-at-rest is for), and env is the leakiest delivery mechanism regardless.

items.prompt: trivy reports 30 MEDIUM CVEs, all in packages your Go binary never touches (perl, vim-common). Durable fix?
items.answer: Rebuild on a distroless or minimal base so those packages aren't in the image at all.
items.explain: Patching packages you don't need is treadmill work; removing them eliminates the findings permanently.

items.prompt: You need to exec into a distroless container to debug a crash, but there's no shell. What do you do?
items.answer: Deploy/debug with a debug-tag variant (distroless debug or busybox), or use kubectl debug with an ephemeral debug container sharing the pod's namespaces.
items.explain: Keep prod distroless; debug via a variant image or ephemeral containers — never by shipping a shell to production.

items.prompt: Your cluster admits only signed images. A developer pushes myapp:latest unsigned from their laptop. What happens at deploy?
items.answer: The admission controller rejects the pod — no valid cosign signature for that digest — and the deploy fails closed.
items.explain: Signature verification fails closed: unsigned means untrusted, regardless of tag.

items.prompt: A new OpenSSL CVE is announced. You have SBOMs for every image. What is your first query?
items.answer: 'Which of my images contain openssl at a vulnerable version?' — answered directly from the stored SBOMs, then rebuild and re-sign those images.
items.explain: The SBOM turns a fire drill into a lookup: scope the blast radius in minutes instead of rescanning everything.

handsOnLab.title: Harden a Container Image End to End
handsOnLab.brief: Take a deliberately insecure sample web app image and harden it through the full pipeline: scan it, shrink it with a multi-stage distroless build, drop root, lock the filesystem read-only, move the secret off the environment, and sign the result.
steps: Build the starter image from the provided Dockerfile (single-stage, root user, secret in ENV) and record its size with docker images.
Run trivy image against the starter image; save the report and count CRITICAL/HIGH findings.
Rewrite the Dockerfile as a multi-stage build: compile/package in a full builder stage, copy only the artifact into a distroless final stage.
Add a non-root USER in the final stage; chown any directories the app must write, or plan volume mounts for them.
Rebuild, compare the new size to the starter, and re-scan with trivy; confirm the finding count dropped.
Run the hardened image with docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp; verify the app starts and serves traffic.
Remove the ENV secret from the Dockerfile; pass the secret as a mounted file instead and confirm the app reads it.
Run docker inspect on the running container and confirm the secret value appears nowhere in the output.
Sign the final image with cosign and record the digest; verify the signature with cosign verify.
Write a one-page hardening checklist (layers, scan gate, non-root, read-only, secret handling, SBOM, signing) your team could adopt.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Hardened multi-stage Dockerfile, before/after trivy reports with finding counts, signed image digest with verification output, and the one-page checklist.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Final image is smaller than the starter, trivy shows zero CRITICAL/HIGH, the container runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, docker inspect reveals no secret, and cosign verify passes.

mockTask.q: Panel: your Dockerfile installs build dependencies with apt-get, compiles the app, then removes the dependencies in a later RUN layer. You claim the final image is minimal. The panelist asks whether the removed packages still ship in the image. What is the correct answer?
choices: No — RUN rm deletes the files from the image permanently
Yes — the removal only adds whiteout markers; the package bytes remain in the earlier layer and are downloadable
No — Docker garbage-collects unreferenced layer content at build time
Yes — but only the file names ship, not their contents
mockTask.explain: Layers are immutable: a later RUN rm creates whiteout markers hiding the files from the container's view, but every byte of the earlier layer ships in the image. The correct fix is chaining install+cleanup in one RUN or, better, a multi-stage build. Answer as if not reading: state the mechanism (whiteout), the consequence (bytes still downloadable), and the fix — that is the full-credit panel answer.

title: Kubernetes Architecture & kubectl
summary: How a Kubernetes cluster is put together — control plane, nodes, kubelet, kube-proxy — and the kubectl fluency (get, describe, logs, exec, contexts, namespaces, events) every troubleshooting session starts with.
objectives: Describe each control-plane component and what it does when a workload is submitted
Explain the roles of kubelet, kube-proxy, and the container runtime on a node
Use kubectl get, describe, logs, and exec to inspect workloads and read cluster state
Work across namespaces and contexts without acting on the wrong cluster
Read cluster events as the primary journal for understanding what the cluster did and why

notes.title: The Control Plane: Four Components, One Job
notes.body: The control plane is the cluster's brain: kube-apiserver (the only component everything talks to — all reads and writes go through its REST API), etcd (the consistent key-value store holding the entire desired state of the cluster), kube-scheduler (assigns unscheduled pods to nodes), and kube-controller-manager (runs reconciliation loops like the ReplicaSet controller). Worked example: you run kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml requesting 3 replicas. Trace the flow: kubectl POSTs to the api-server, which validates and writes the Deployment to etcd; the Deployment controller notices and creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates 3 Pod objects (still unscheduled); the scheduler watches for unscheduled pods, scores the nodes, and binds each pod to a node by writing the binding through the api-server. Solution to 'which component scheduled my pod?': the scheduler — and every step was a watch-and-react loop against state in etcd, which is why 'the cluster converges' instead of 'commands execute'.

notes.title: Nodes: kubelet, kube-proxy, Container Runtime
notes.body: Nodes are the muscle. Each node runs kubelet (the agent that ensures the containers described in pod specs are actually running — pulling images, starting containers, running probes, reporting status back), kube-proxy (maintains network rules so Service virtual IPs route to the right pods), and a container runtime (containerd, which does the actual container lifecycle). Worked example: the scheduler binds your pod to node worker-2. The kubelet on worker-2 sees the new pod spec via its watch on the api-server, asks containerd to pull nginx:1.25, starts the container, begins running the configured liveness probe, and reports the pod phase back as Running. Meanwhile kube-proxy on every node updates its iptables/IPVS rules so the Service's ClusterIP now includes the new pod's IP. If the container crashes, it is the kubelet — not the scheduler — that restarts it, because the kubelet owns the pod's actual state on that node.

notes.title: kubectl get, describe, logs, exec
notes.body: These four commands are 90% of daily Kubernetes work, and each answers a different question. Worked example: users report the checkout page is down. You run kubectl get pods -n shop and see checkout-7d9c8f-abcde in CrashLoopBackOff with 14 restarts — get tells you WHAT the state is. kubectl describe pod checkout-7d9c8f-abcde -n shop shows the Events section: 'Back-off restarting failed container' and under Containers, Last State: Terminated with exit code 1 — describe tells you WHY the cluster thinks it's happening. kubectl logs checkout-7d9c8f-abcde -n shop --previous shows 'FATAL: could not connect to postgres:5432' — logs tell you what the APPLICATION says. kubectl exec -it checkout-7d9c8f-abcde -n shop -- sh lets you test DNS and connectivity from inside — exec lets you investigate live. Solution: the database hostname changed; fix the env var. Learn the order — get, describe, logs, exec — and you will triage faster than anyone reaching for dashboards first.

notes.title: Namespaces and Contexts: Not Acting on the Wrong Cluster
notes.body: Namespaces partition one cluster (dev, staging, prod, or team boundaries); contexts bundle a cluster + user + namespace into a named entry in your kubeconfig so one kubectl can talk to many clusters. Worked example: your kubeconfig has contexts aks-prod, aks-dev, and kind-local. You intend to delete a test pod in dev but your current context is aks-prod — kubectl delete pod test-xyz would hit production. Solution: make context-switching deliberate: kubectl config get-contexts to see the starred current context, kubectl config use-context aks-dev to switch, and always scope with -n dev. Better, set a per-shell default namespace (kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev) and use tools that show the current context in your prompt. The panel-relevant habit: before any destructive command, run kubectl config current-context and confirm the namespace — 'I deleted prod' is a career-defining sentence.

notes.title: Events: The Cluster's Journal
notes.body: Events are the cluster's own log of what it did and why — scheduling decisions, image pulls, probe failures, evictions — and they expire (typically after an hour), so they are a 'what just happened' tool, not an audit trail. Worked example: kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' shows: 'FailedScheduling: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory', then 'Successfully assigned shop/checkout-xyz to worker-2', then 'Failed to pull image "myapp:v9": rpc error: image not found'. Solution reading: the pod first couldn't schedule (nodes full), then a node freed up and it was assigned, and now it's failing on a bad image tag — three distinct problems visible in one command, each pointing at a different fix (add capacity or reduce requests; fix the tag). Pair events with describe: describe shows the events for one object inline, while get events --sort-by across a namespace shows the cluster's recent story in time order.

notes.title: Declarative State and Reconciliation
notes.body: You never tell Kubernetes HOW to do something — you declare the desired state ('3 replicas of this pod') and controllers loop forever driving actual state toward it. Worked example: a Deployment wants 3 replicas; node worker-3 dies with one replica on it. The node controller marks the node NotReady, the pods on it go Unknown, and after the toleration timeout the ReplicaSet controller sees actual (2) < desired (3) and creates a replacement pod, which the scheduler binds to a healthy node. You did nothing — the loop closed itself. Solution to the common confusion 'why did Kubernetes create a pod I didn't ask for?': you asked for 3 replicas, declaratively, and the controller is honoring your declaration. This mental model is the prerequisite for everything in M27-M31: troubleshooting is asking 'which controller is unhappy, and what actual-vs-desired gap is it reporting?'

cards.front: Name the four control-plane components and one-line each.
cards.back: kube-apiserver (all API traffic), etcd (stores all cluster state), kube-scheduler (assigns pods to nodes), kube-controller-manager (reconciliation loops).

cards.front: What does etcd store, and why does its health matter?
cards.back: The entire desired and actual state of the cluster. If etcd is unhealthy or loses quorum, the api-server cannot serve reads/writes and the cluster is effectively down.

cards.front: Which component decides WHICH node a pod lands on?
cards.back: kube-scheduler — it watches for unscheduled pods, scores feasible nodes, and writes the binding.

cards.front: What does kubelet do? What does kube-proxy do?
cards.back: kubelet: runs the pod's containers on its node (pull, start, probe, report status, restart on crash). kube-proxy: maintains network rules so Service IPs route to healthy pods.

cards.front: kubectl get vs kubectl describe — what question does each answer?
cards.back: get: WHAT is the current state (terse table). describe: WHY — full object detail plus the Events section explaining recent cluster actions.

cards.front: How do you see a crashed container's logs, and how do you get a shell in a running one?
cards.back: kubectl logs <pod> --previous for the crashed container's output; kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh for a shell.

cards.front: What is a namespace? What is a context?
cards.back: Namespace: a partition of one cluster (dev/staging/prod, teams). Context: a named kubeconfig entry bundling cluster + user + namespace.

cards.front: Before running a destructive kubectl command, what two things do you verify?
cards.back: kubectl config current-context (right cluster) and the target namespace (-n flag or current default).

cards.front: What are Kubernetes Events and how long do they live?
cards.back: The cluster's journal of actions and reasons (scheduling, pulls, probe failures). They expire — typically ~1 hour — so they're for recent history, not auditing.

cards.front: Command to see recent events across a namespace in time order?
cards.back: kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'

cards.front: A node dies with one replica of a 3-replica Deployment on it. Who creates the replacement, and did you need to act?
cards.back: The ReplicaSet controller notices actual < desired and creates a replacement pod; the scheduler binds it. No action needed — reconciliation closes the loop.

cards.front: All kubectl traffic flows through which single component?
cards.back: kube-apiserver — every component, including kubectl and the controllers, talks only to the api-server.

quiz.q: You kubectl apply a Deployment with 3 replicas. Which component assigns the resulting pods to nodes?
choices: kube-controller-manager
kube-scheduler
kubelet
etcd
quiz.explain: The scheduler watches for unscheduled pods and binds each to a node. The controller-manager creates the pod objects; kubelet runs them once bound.

quiz.q: Where is the cluster's entire state stored?
choices: In the kube-apiserver's memory
In etcd, a consistent key-value store
On each node's local disk
In the kube-scheduler's cache
quiz.explain: etcd holds all desired and actual state; the api-server is stateless and reads/writes etcd. Lose etcd quorum and the cluster stops functioning.

quiz.q: A container keeps crashing. Which command shows the crashed container's output?
choices: kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl describe node
kubectl get events --all-namespaces
kubectl exec <pod> -- dmesg
quiz.explain: --previous fetches logs from the last terminated container instance — exactly what you need when the current one has already been replaced by a restart.

quiz.q: kubectl get pods shows a pod Running, but describe shows repeated 'Liveness probe failed' events. Who will restart the container?
choices: The scheduler, by rescheduling the pod
kubelet, on the node where the pod runs
The Deployment controller
kube-proxy
quiz.explain: kubelet owns the pod's actual state on its node: it runs probes and restarts containers whose liveness probe fails.

quiz.q: You have contexts aks-prod and aks-dev. How do you make certain your next command targets dev?
choices: kubectl config use-context aks-dev, then verify with current-context
kubectl delete context aks-prod
Edit /etc/hosts to point prod at dev
Add --force to every command
quiz.explain: Switch the current context explicitly and verify — the starred context in get-contexts is what every subsequent command uses.

quiz.q: Events show 'FailedScheduling: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory'. What does this mean and what fixes it?
choices: The image is too large; use a smaller tag
No node has enough free memory for the pod's requests; reduce requests, free capacity, or add nodes
etcd is full; compact it
The namespace quota is exceeded; delete the namespace
quiz.explain: The scheduler found zero feasible nodes because each node's allocatable memory minus existing requests is less than this pod's memory request.

quiz.q: Which statement about the container runtime (containerd) is correct?
choices: It schedules pods to nodes
It stores cluster state
It performs the actual container lifecycle — pull, create, start, stop — at kubelet's direction
It routes Service traffic
quiz.explain: containerd is the low-level runtime; kubelet instructs it, and kube-proxy handles Service routing.

quiz.q: A pod you never created appears in the namespace. Most likely explanation?
choices: Someone hacked the cluster
A controller (e.g. ReplicaSet) created it to satisfy a declared desired state
The scheduler creates pods spontaneously
etcd replicates pods automatically
quiz.explain: Declarative model: you declared 3 replicas, a node died, the controller created a replacement. Unexpected pods are almost always reconciliation, not intrusion — verify via ownerReferences.

quiz.q: kubectl exec -it web-abc -- sh hangs with no prompt. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The api-server is down
The container image has no shell (e.g. distroless)
The pod is in another namespace
exec requires root on the node
quiz.explain: Distroless/minimal images ship no /bin/sh, so exec has nothing to launch. Use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container instead.

items.prompt: List all pods in the payments namespace, including ones that finished.
items.answer: kubectl get pods -n payments -a (or --show-all on older versions; completed pods show with -a).
items.explain: get pods defaults to hiding terminated pods in some versions; -a/--show-all includes them. -n scopes the namespace.

items.prompt: Show full details and events for pod api-7f9c4 in namespace shop.
items.answer: kubectl describe pod api-7f9c4 -n shop
items.explain: describe renders the full object plus the Events section — the single richest triage command.

items.prompt: A pod has two containers, web and sidecar. Get logs for sidecar only.
items.answer: kubectl logs <pod> -c sidecar -n <ns>
items.explain: -c selects the container; without it, logs defaults to the first/only container.

items.prompt: Open an interactive shell in the running pod cache-xyz in namespace infra.
items.answer: kubectl exec -it cache-xyz -n infra -- sh
items.explain: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY, -- separates kubectl flags from the command.

items.prompt: Switch your shell to the aks-staging context and set its default namespace to api.
items.answer: kubectl config use-context aks-staging && kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=api
items.explain: use-context changes cluster+user; set-context --current --namespace changes the default namespace for that context.

items.prompt: Show the last 20 events in namespace shop, newest last.
items.answer: kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20
items.explain: Events sort by lastTimestamp; piping to tail shows the most recent. Events expire, so this is recent-history only.

items.prompt: List nodes with their internal IPs and Kubernetes versions.
items.answer: kubectl get nodes -o wide
items.explain: -o wide adds IPs, OS image, and versions to the default node table — the fastest node inventory.

items.prompt: Pods stay Pending with 'no nodes available'. Which component made that decision, and where do you read its reasoning?
items.answer: kube-scheduler; its reasoning is in the pod's Events (kubectl describe pod).
items.explain: Only the scheduler binds pods; its FailedScheduling events name the exact predicate that failed (resources, taints, affinity).

items.prompt: You apply a Deployment and no ReplicaSet appears. Which component failed, and what do you check?
items.answer: kube-controller-manager's Deployment controller; check its logs and the Deployment's status/events for validation errors.
items.explain: Controller-manager runs the Deployment→ReplicaSet loop; if the Deployment object is malformed the api-server would have rejected it at apply time.

items.prompt: A Service's ClusterIP doesn't route to a new pod. Which node component owns that programming?
items.answer: kube-proxy on each node (iptables/IPVS rules); verify with iptables-save or ipvsadm on the node, and check the Service's Endpoints.
items.explain: kube-proxy translates Service abstractions into node-level forwarding rules; missing Endpoints means the selector matched no pods.

items.prompt: kubectl commands hang cluster-wide. Which two components do you suspect first?
items.answer: kube-apiserver (all traffic flows through it) and etcd (its backing store / quorum).
items.explain: Every kubectl call is an api-server call backed by etcd; cluster-wide hangs point at one of these two, not at workloads.

items.prompt: A container crashes and restarts without any new pod being created. Who restarted it?
items.answer: kubelet on that node, per the pod's restartPolicy.
items.explain: Container restarts are kubelet's job; pod replacement (new pod object) is the controller's job. Restart count increments on the same pod.

items.prompt: Two teams share a cluster and team A's pods see team B's ConfigMaps. What construct should have isolated them?
items.answer: Namespaces — with RBAC limiting each team to its own namespace.
items.explain: Namespaces are the isolation boundary; without them (and RBAC), everything in the cluster is visible to everyone with API access.

items.prompt: You need to prove which user applied a change last Tuesday. Do Events suffice?
items.answer: No — Events expire (~1 hour) and don't record the actor reliably. Use api-server audit logs.
items.explain: Events are operational journal, not audit trail. Audit policy + log backend is the compliance answer.

handsOnLab.title: Stand Up a Cluster and Learn kubectl
handsOnLab.brief: Create a local kind cluster, deploy a sample app across namespaces, and practice the full kubectl inspection loop — get, describe, logs, exec, events — plus safe context handling.
steps: Install kind and kubectl; create a cluster with kind create cluster --name lab and verify with kubectl cluster-info.
Create namespaces lab-dev and lab-prod; confirm with kubectl get namespaces.
Deploy the nginx:1.25 Deployment manifest into lab-dev with 2 replicas; watch pods become Running.
Run kubectl get pods -n lab-dev -o wide and record each pod's node and IP.
Run kubectl describe pod on one replica; identify the Events section and the node it was scheduled to.
Fetch logs with kubectl logs, then exec into the pod and run hostname and cat /etc/os-release.
Create a second context entry pointing at the same cluster with default namespace lab-prod (use kubectl config set-context).
Switch between contexts with use-context and verify the active one each time with current-context.
Generate activity (scale the Deployment, delete a pod) and read the story back with kubectl get events --sort-by.
Delete the kind cluster; document the five commands you would run first in any future triage.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A triage runbook (the five first commands) plus terminal transcripts showing get/describe/logs/exec/events output from your lab cluster.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can switch contexts without hesitation, explain every line of a describe output, and retrieve previous-container logs on demand.

mockTask.q: Panel: the on-call engineer reports 'the app is down' and shows you kubectl get pods with the pod in CrashLoopBackOff. They ask what you run next, in order. What is the correct triage sequence?
choices: kubectl exec into the pod, then restart the Deployment, then check logs
kubectl describe pod (events + last state), then kubectl logs --previous (crashed output), then kubectl exec (live probing)
Delete the pod immediately so the controller recreates it fresh
kubectl get nodes, then drain the node, then re-apply the manifest
mockTask.explain: The order is get (what), describe (why per the cluster: events + exit code/last state), logs --previous (what the app said as it died), exec (live investigation only if the container stays up). Deleting or restarting before reading evidence destroys the data you need — the panel wants the disciplined sequence, narrated as you go.

videos.title: Kubernetes Tutorial for Beginners [FULL COURSE in 4 Hours]
videos.blurb: The well-known full-length walkthrough of Kubernetes architecture and kubectl — watch the architecture and core-objects sections to anchor this module's notes.

title: Pod Lifecycle & Troubleshooting
summary: The pod lifecycle from Pending to Running to failure — plus the two runbooks every on-call engineer needs: Pending/scheduling failures and CrashLoopBackOff, and the full panel answer to 'the pod keeps restarting, what are your next steps?'
objectives: Name the pod phases and explain what Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, and Unknown each mean
Apply the triage order — describe/events, logs, exec — to any failing pod without guessing
Work the CrashLoopBackOff runbook: read backoff timing, last state, and previous logs to find root cause
Work the Pending runbook: interpret scheduler events for resources, taints, and affinity failures
Deliver the full panel answer for 'pod keeps restarting' with a narrated, ordered investigation

notes.title: Pod Phases: The Five States
notes.body: A pod is always in exactly one phase: Pending (accepted by the cluster but at least one container not yet running — includes scheduling and image pulling), Running (all containers created, at least one running — note this does NOT mean the app is healthy), Succeeded (all containers terminated with exit 0 — jobs), Failed (at least one container terminated non-zero), Unknown (the node stopped reporting — the api-server genuinely doesn't know). Worked example: kubectl get pods shows web-abc as Running for 20 minutes, yet the app serves 500s. A learner says 'the pod is fine, must be the code.' Solution: Running only means the processes started — readiness probes, not phase, determine whether traffic flows. The panel lesson: never equate Running with healthy; always pair phase with probe status, restart count, and logs. Unknown deserves special respect: it usually means the node died, and the pod may actually still be running orphaned on it.

notes.title: The Triage Order: Describe, Logs, Exec
notes.body: When a pod misbehaves, run the same sequence every time so you never destroy evidence: 1) kubectl describe pod — read Events (what the cluster did) and container Statuses (restart count, last termination reason and exit code); 2) kubectl logs --previous — what the application printed as it died; 3) kubectl logs (current) — what it's saying now; 4) kubectl exec — live probing only if a container stays up long enough. Worked example: api-xyz is CrashLoopBackOff, 22 restarts. describe shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1, and Events: 'Back-off restarting failed container'. logs --previous shows 'FATAL: password authentication failed for user "api"'. Solution: the database credential rotated; update the Secret the pod consumes. If you had exec'd first or deleted the pod, the --previous logs would be gone. Discipline beats speed: evidence first, action second.

notes.title: CrashLoopBackOff Runbook
notes.body: CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts, exits non-zero, and kubelet is backing off before retrying: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s, capped at 300s (5 minutes) between attempts. Worked example: you watch kubectl get pods and the pod flaps between CrashLoopBackOff and Running every few minutes; describe shows restartCount: 31 and Last State exit code 1. The naive fix is 'increase resources' — but exit code 1 is an application error, not OOM (which would be 137). Solution path: logs --previous reveals 'bind: address already in use :8080' — a second process in the container is grabbing the port, an image build issue, not a cluster issue. The runbook: note the exit code (1=app error, 2=misuse, 126/127=command not found, 137=SIGKILL/OOM, 139=segfault, 143=SIGTERM), read previous logs, check the command/args and env, then fix the image or config — never 'fix' CrashLoopBackOff by deleting the pod, which resets the backoff timer and your evidence.

notes.title: Pending Runbook: Reading Scheduler Events
notes.body: A pod stuck in Pending was accepted but the scheduler cannot place it — the reason is always in Events. Worked example: kubectl describe pod shows '0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had taint {dedicated: gpu}, 2 Insufficient memory.' Solution: this single event names two distinct problems — one node is tainted for GPU workloads (add a toleration only if this pod belongs there), and the other two lack free memory for the pod's requests (lower the request if over-provisioned, or add capacity). Common Pending causes to memorize: Insufficient cpu/memory (requests too high), node taints without tolerations, nodeSelector/affinity matching no nodes, PersistentVolumeClaims unbound (storage class or capacity), and ImagePullBackOff (wrong tag or missing imagePullSecrets — technically a Pending sub-state). The fix is never to force-schedule; it's to resolve what the scheduler is telling you.

notes.title: Exit Codes and Last State
notes.body: The container's exit code is the single most informative number in pod troubleshooting, and describe pod surfaces it under lastState.terminated. Worked example: three pods, three failures. Pod A: exit 1, logs show a Python traceback — application bug, fix the code. Pod B: exit 137, Reason OOMKilled — the container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it (137 = 128 + 9, SIGKILL); fix by raising the limit or cutting memory use. Pod C: exit 143 (128 + 15, SIGTERM) right after a deployment — normal graceful shutdown during a rolling update, not a failure at all. Solution discipline: read the code before the logs. 137 always means killed from outside (OOM or manual kill), never an app crash; 143 during deploys is expected; 1/2 are yours to debug in the application. Misreading 137 as 'the app crashed' sends teams chasing code bugs for a resource problem.

notes.title: Panel Question: 'The Pod Keeps Restarting — Next Steps?'
notes.body: This is the signature panel question for this module — answer it as a narrated sequence, not a list of commands. Model answer: 'First I'd run kubectl get pods to confirm the restart count is climbing and note the status — CrashLoopBackOff versus Error tells me whether kubelet is backing off. Then kubectl describe pod: I read the Events for the cluster's view and the container's lastState for the exit code and reason — 137 points at memory, 1 points at the app. Then kubectl logs --previous to see what the application printed as it died, because the current container may already be gone. If it stays up long enough, I'd exec in and check the process, env, and connectivity. Then I fix the root cause — bad image tag, missing env var, failed probe, OOM — and verify the restart count stops climbing.' Worked example of full credit: the candidate who says 'exit 137, so I checked the memory limit in describe, confirmed OOMKilled in lastState, and raised the limit' demonstrates the whole chain. Practice saying this aloud until it's automatic — panels score the order and the reasoning, not just the commands.

cards.front: Name the five pod phases and what Pending means.
cards.back: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown. Pending: accepted by the cluster, at least one container not yet running (scheduling, pulling, or initializing).

cards.front: Does pod phase Running mean the application is healthy?
cards.back: No — it only means the containers started. Health is determined by readiness probes; a Running pod can serve 500s.

cards.front: State the pod triage order and what each step answers.
cards.back: describe (cluster's view: events, exit code, last state) → logs --previous (what the app said dying) → logs (current) → exec (live probing). Evidence before action.

cards.front: What is the CrashLoopBackOff backoff sequence?
cards.back: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s, capped at 300s (5 min) between restart attempts.

cards.front: Decode these exit codes: 1, 2, 126, 137, 139, 143.
cards.back: 1 app error; 2 misuse of shell builtin; 126 command not executable; 137 SIGKILL (OOMKilled); 139 segfault (128+11); 143 SIGTERM graceful (128+15).

cards.front: Exit code 137 with Reason OOMKilled — what happened and what are the two fixes?
cards.back: The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it. Raise the memory limit or reduce the app's memory footprint.

cards.front: Pod stuck Pending, event: '0/3 nodes available: 3 Insufficient cpu'. Meaning and fixes?
cards.back: No node has enough free CPU for the pod's cpu request. Lower the request if over-provisioned, free capacity, or add nodes.

cards.front: Pod stuck Pending, event mentions a taint. What is the fix?
cards.back: Add a matching toleration to the pod — but only if the pod belongs on the tainted nodes; otherwise schedule elsewhere.

cards.front: What does ImagePullBackOff mean and what are the two usual causes?
cards.back: kubelet cannot pull the container image. Usual causes: wrong image tag / nonexistent image, or missing imagePullSecrets for a private registry.

cards.front: Why must you check logs --previous BEFORE deleting a crashing pod?
cards.back: Deleting the pod destroys the terminated container and its logs — the evidence of why it died goes with it.

cards.front: Pod phase Unknown — what does it mean and what usually caused it?
cards.back: The node stopped reporting; the api-server genuinely doesn't know the pod's state. Usually the node died or lost network.

cards.front: First three sentences of your panel answer to 'the pod keeps restarting'?
cards.back: 'I'd check the restart count and status, then describe the pod for events and the exit code in lastState, then read the previous container's logs — in that order, before touching anything.'

quiz.q: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff with restartCount 31. What is the FIRST command in your triage?
choices: kubectl delete pod to force a fresh start
kubectl describe pod — read Events and the container's lastState (exit code/reason)
kubectl exec into the pod to check the app
kubectl drain the node
quiz.explain: describe gives the cluster's view (events) plus the exit code and termination reason — the evidence that directs everything after. Deleting destroys evidence; exec likely fails on a crashing container.

quiz.q: describe shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Root cause?
choices: Application bug — fix the code
The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
The node ran out of disk
The liveness probe failed
quiz.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); OOMKilled means the kernel killed the process for exceeding its cgroup memory limit. Fix: raise the limit or reduce memory use.

quiz.q: logs --previous shows 'FATAL: password authentication failed for user "api"'. What is the fix?
choices: Increase the pod's memory limit
Update the database credential in the Secret the pod consumes
Add a liveness probe
Pull the image again
quiz.explain: The app is failing on a bad/rotated DB credential — a config problem, not a resource or probe problem. Update the Secret and the pod picks it up on restart.

quiz.q: Pod Pending with event '1 node(s) had taint {dedicated: gpu}, 2 Insufficient memory'. How many distinct problems, and what are they?
choices: One: the cluster is full
Two: a taint blocking one node, and insufficient free memory on the other two for this pod's requests
One: the GPU taint — remove it
Two: the image is bad and the node is down
quiz.explain: Read the event literally: the taint excludes one node (needs a toleration), and the other two lack memory headroom for the pod's requests. Each needs its own fix.

quiz.q: During a rolling deployment you see pods terminate with exit code 143. What should you do?
choices: Page the on-call — containers are crashing
Nothing — 143 is SIGTERM, the normal graceful shutdown during a rolling update
Increase memory limits immediately
Roll back the deployment
quiz.explain: 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM). Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to old pods during rollouts; graceful shutdown exits 143 by design. Only investigate if the new pods fail to become ready.

quiz.q: A pod is Running but serves errors. Which check determines whether it receives traffic?
choices: The pod phase
The restart count
The readiness probe status and the Service's Endpoints list
The node's kubelet logs
quiz.explain: Running only means started. Endpoints include only pods passing readiness; a failing readiness probe removes the pod from the Service without restarting it.

quiz.q: ImagePullBackOff on a newly deployed pod. Two most likely causes?
choices: CPU throttling and memory pressure
Wrong image tag (image doesn't exist) or missing imagePullSecrets for the private registry
Taints and affinity rules
Full etcd and api-server overload
quiz.explain: ImagePullBackOff is specifically the kubelet failing to fetch the image — tag typos and absent registry credentials cover nearly all cases.

quiz.q: Why is 'delete the pod and see if it comes back healthy' bad triage for CrashLoopBackOff?
choices: It is actually the recommended first step
It resets the backoff timer and destroys the terminated container's logs — your best evidence
Deleting pods is forbidden by Kubernetes
It always causes data loss
quiz.explain: The controller recreates an identical pod that will crash identically; meanwhile --previous logs are gone. Evidence first, action second.

quiz.q: Events show 'Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500' then the container restarts. Which component restarted it and why?
choices: The scheduler, because the node was unhealthy
kubelet, because a failed liveness probe means 'restart this container'
The Deployment controller, because replicas dropped
kube-proxy, because the Service lost endpoints
quiz.explain: kubelet executes probes; liveness failure = container is dead, restart it. (Readiness failure would only remove it from Endpoints.)

items.prompt: Pod in CrashLoopBackOff. describe shows exit code 1, logs --previous show a Python ModuleNotFoundError. Root cause and fix?
items.answer: The image is missing a Python dependency. Fix: add it to requirements and rebuild the image (or fix the install step).
items.explain: Exit 1 + import error = build/packaging bug, not a cluster problem. The fix is in the Dockerfile, not in kubectl.

items.prompt: Pod in CrashLoopBackOff. describe shows exit 137, Reason OOMKilled, limit 256Mi. Fix?
items.answer: Raise the memory limit (and check the request still schedules), or reduce the app's memory use.
items.explain: 137/OOMKilled is definitive: the cgroup limit was exceeded. Raising the limit is the immediate fix; profiling memory is the durable one.

items.prompt: Pod Pending 10 minutes. Events: '0/5 nodes are available: 5 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity'. Fix?
items.answer: The nodeAffinity rules match no nodes — correct the labels/affinity or label a node appropriately.
items.explain: The scheduler is explicit: affinity selected zero nodes. Either the pod's rules are wrong or the nodes aren't labeled as expected.

items.prompt: Pod Pending. Events: 'persistentvolumeclaim "data" not found' repeated. Fix?
items.answer: The PVC doesn't exist (or is in another namespace) — create it or fix the claimName.
items.explain: Unbound/missing PVC blocks scheduling; the pod waits for storage that never arrives.

items.prompt: Pod Running, 0 restarts, but the Service has no endpoints for it. What do you check?
items.answer: The readiness probe status and whether the pod's labels match the Service selector.
items.explain: No endpoints = failing readiness or selector mismatch. The pod is 'Running' but not ready — phase alone misleads.

items.prompt: After a config change, ALL pods of a Deployment enter CrashLoopBackOff simultaneously with exit 1. Fastest diagnostic?
items.answer: logs --previous on one pod (config errors are identical across replicas) + diff the ConfigMap/Secret change.
items.explain: Simultaneous identical crashes after a config change = the change is the cause; one pod's logs represent all of them.

items.prompt: Pod shows Unknown for 6 minutes after a node reboot. What do you do?
items.answer: Check node status; once the node is NotReady past the pod-eviction timeout, the controller evicts and reschedules. Don't force-delete unless you accept possible duplicate execution.
items.explain: Unknown means the node isn't reporting; force-deleting risks two live copies if the node is actually still running the pod.

items.prompt: Give your opening sentence when the panel says 'a pod keeps restarting — walk me through it'.
items.answer: 'First I'd confirm the restart count is climbing and note the exact status — CrashLoopBackOff, Error, or OOMKilled each points somewhere different.'
items.explain: Panels score the opening: it shows you classify before acting instead of spraying commands.

items.prompt: After confirming restarts, what do you run and what two things do you read from it?
items.answer: kubectl describe pod — the Events section (cluster's actions/reasons) and the container's lastState (exit code + termination reason).
items.explain: This one command separates resource kills (137) from app errors (1) from probe kills — the branch point of the whole investigation.

items.prompt: Exit code is 1. What is your next command and what are you looking for?
items.answer: kubectl logs <pod> --previous — the application's own output as it died: tracebacks, connection errors, config complaints.
items.explain: Exit 1 is the app's fault; only the app's logs say which fault. --previous is critical because the current container may be a fresh crashed loop.

items.prompt: Exit code is 137, Reason OOMKilled. State your conclusion and fix in two sentences.
items.answer: 'The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it. I'd raise the memory limit to fit the workload — or reduce the app's footprint — and verify the restart count stops climbing.'
items.explain: Name the mechanism (cgroup OOM kill), give both fix directions, state the verification. That's a complete panel answer.

items.prompt: The pod stays up 30 seconds then dies, too fast for exec. How do you still investigate live state?
items.answer: You don't — you rely on describe + previous logs, and add a temporary sleep/debug command or kubectl debug ephemeral container if you must inspect the filesystem.
items.explain: Chasing a 30-second window with exec is flailing; the evidence commands plus a slowed-down repro are the professional path.

items.prompt: You've found the root cause (bad env var). What are your closing sentences to the panel?
items.answer: 'I'd fix the value in the Secret/ConfigMap, roll the Deployment so pods pick it up, and watch the restart count and readiness go green — then add a startup probe or config validation so this fails fast next time.'
items.explain: Close the loop: fix, verify, and prevent recurrence. Panels reward the prevention sentence.

items.prompt: The panel asks: 'When would you NOT follow this sequence?' Give one valid exception.
items.answer: An active security incident (compromised pod) — then you isolate/quarantine first (network policy, cordon) and investigate from forensic copies, because evidence preservation and containment outrank root-cause order.
items.explain: Shows judgment: the triage order serves availability debugging; security incidents have their own playbook where containment comes first.

handsOnLab.title: Break Pods and Triage Them
handsOnLab.brief: Deploy four deliberately broken pods — bad image tag, crashing command, missing env var, unsatisfiable scheduling constraint — and work each through the triage order, documenting evidence and root cause before fixing.
steps: Create namespace triage-lab; deploy pod bad-image with image nginx:nonexistent-tag and observe ImagePullBackOff.
Run the full triage on bad-image: describe (events), and record the exact error message.
Deploy pod crash-cmd with command ['sh','-c','exit 1']; watch it enter CrashLoopBackOff and note the backoff intervals.
Triage crash-cmd: describe for exit code, logs --previous for output; record both.
Deploy pod missing-env referencing a Secret key that doesn't exist; observe CreateContainerConfigError and triage via describe.
Deploy pod no-fit with nodeSelector {disktype: ssd} on nodes without that label; observe Pending and read the scheduler event.
Fix all four (correct tag, valid command, create the Secret, remove/fix the nodeSelector) and verify each reaches Running.
For crash-cmd, temporarily set a memory limit of 32Mi on a memory-hungry variant; observe OOMKilled/137 in lastState.
Write the triage order on an index card from memory; then re-triage one pod using only the card.
Document each scenario as: symptom → evidence commands → root cause → fix, in a one-page runbook.
handsOnLab.deliverable: One-page runbook covering the four broken-pod scenarios plus the OOMKilled case, each with symptom, evidence, root cause, and fix.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can name the root cause of any of the five broken pods from describe + logs output alone, and you recite the triage order without notes.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'A pod keeps restarting. Walk me through your next steps.' Which response earns full credit?
choices: 'I'd delete the pod so the controller recreates it, then watch if the new one stays up.'
'I'd check the restart count and status, describe the pod for events and the exit code in lastState, read the previous container's logs, and only then exec or fix — matching the fix to the evidence.'
'I'd immediately scale the Deployment to zero and re-apply the manifests.'
'I'd drain the node and cordon it, since restarts are usually node problems.'
mockTask.explain: Full credit is the ordered, evidence-first narration: get (classify), describe (events + exit code = branch point), logs --previous (app's dying words), then targeted action. Deleting destroys evidence; draining assumes a node cause with no data. Deliver it as a spoken sequence — panels score order and reasoning.
