title: Resources: Requests/Limits, OOMKilled/Exit 137 & Probes
summary: How Kubernetes divides CPU and memory between containers — requests, limits, millicores, and the OOM killer — plus the three probes (startup, readiness, liveness) and how to tune them, built around the real panel YAML-review and exit-137 questions.
objectives: Distinguish CPU/memory requests from limits and predict scheduling and throttling behavior
Review a pod resource spec (the panel's nginx YAML) and identify what breaks in production
Diagnose OOMKilled / exit code 137 from lastState and choose the correct fix
Assign startup, readiness, and liveness probes to the right job and explain what each failure does
Tune probe parameters and explain single-threaded readiness failures such as the Python GIL case

notes.title: Requests vs Limits: Two Different Promises
notes.body: Requests are what the scheduler uses: 'this container needs at least this much to be placeable.' Limits are what the kernel enforces: 'this container may never exceed this much.' CPU is compressible (throttled when over limit); memory is incompressible (exceed the limit and the kernel OOM-kills the process). Worked example: a node has 4 CPUs (4000 millicores) and 16 Gi memory free. You submit pods requesting 500m CPU / 1Gi memory each. How many schedule? By CPU: 4000/500 = 8; by memory: 16/1 = 16 — the scheduler takes the tighter constraint, so 8 pods schedule (bin-packing across both dimensions). If each pod's CPU limit is 2000m, all 8 can still burst to 2 cores when idle CPU exists — limits don't reserve, they cap. Solution to the classic confusion: requests determine PLACEMENT, limits determine ENFORCEMENT, and over-requesting is the #1 cause of 'the cluster is full but nothing is busy.'

notes.title: Panel Exercise: Review This nginx YAML
notes.body: The panel shows a frontend pod: image nginx:v4, requests {memory: 16Gi, cpu: 0.5}, limits {memory: 32Gi, cpu: 8}. 'What issues will this cause later?' Worked analysis: an nginx frontend requesting 16 Gi of memory is absurd — nginx typically needs tens of MB — so each replica consumes a huge scheduling reservation; a 3-replica Deployment reserves 48 Gi of cluster memory for a web server, starving real workloads and triggering 'Insufficient memory' Pending events elsewhere. The 8-CPU limit lets one pod burst to 8 cores, so under load this frontend can throttle neighboring pods' CPU (noisy neighbor), while the 0.5-CPU request means it scheduled onto nearly-empty CPU nodes that its memory request then hogs. Solution you'd propose: right-size to requests like {memory: 128Mi, cpu: 100m} and limits like {memory: 256Mi, cpu: 500m}, measured from actual usage (kubectl top, metrics history), and set namespace LimitRanges so no one can submit 16Gi requests again. The panel is testing whether you spot over-requesting as a cluster-wide hazard, not just a wasteful pod.

notes.title: Request 1Gi but the App Needs 2Gi: Does It Start?
notes.body: Panel follow-up: 'nginx needs a minimum of 2Gi to start. The request is 1Gi. Does it work?' Worked reasoning: the scheduler only looks at requests, so YES, the pod schedules — 1Gi fits on any node with 1Gi free. What happens next depends on the limit. Case A: limit is also 1Gi — the container starts, memory climbs past 1Gi during startup, the kernel OOM-kills it: CrashLoopBackOff with exit 137, Reason OOMKilled. Case B: no limit set — the container starts, uses 2Gi+, and survives until the NODE comes under memory pressure, at which point the kubelet evicts the pod (it exceeded its request, making it the first eviction candidate). Solution: requests must reflect reality — set the request at or above the app's actual minimum (2Gi) so scheduling is honest, and set the limit slightly above the request to absorb spikes. 'It schedules' is not 'it works.'

notes.title: OOMKilled and Exit 137: Diagnosis via Last State
notes.body: Exit code 137 means the process was SIGKILLed (128 + 9) — it did not crash on its own; something killed it. In Kubernetes that something is almost always the kernel's OOM killer enforcing the container's memory limit, recorded as Reason: OOMKilled in the container's lastState. Worked example: container svc-basic terminated with exit code 137. You run kubectl describe pod and read: Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, Started/Finished timestamps 40 seconds apart, restartCount climbing. The app's previous logs show normal startup then silence — no traceback, because the kernel gave no warning. Solution: confirm the limit (describe shows limits.memory: 512Mi), check actual usage trend (kubectl top pod / metrics), then either raise the limit to cover the real working set or fix the memory growth (leak, unbounded cache). Never 'fix' 137 by adding CPU or restarting the node — it's a memory-limit event, full stop.

notes.title: The Three Probes: Startup, Readiness, Liveness
notes.body: Probes are kubelet-run health checks, and each answers a different question. Startup probe: 'has the app finished initializing?' — while it fails, liveness/readiness are disabled, so slow-starting apps (JVM warmup) don't get killed mid-boot. Readiness probe: 'is the app ready for traffic?' — failure removes the pod from Service Endpoints WITHOUT restarting it. Liveness probe: 'is the app still alive?' — failure RESTARTS the container. Worked example (panel question): a pod runs fine for an hour, then suddenly restarts with no code change. Which probe? Solution: liveness — it's the only probe that restarts a running container. A readiness failure would have just pulled it from the Service silently. The panel's deeper test: 'the app deadlocks but the process lives' — liveness must test actual function (e.g. HTTP /healthz that exercises the request path), not just 'process exists', or the deadlock never triggers a restart.

notes.title: Probe Tuning and the Python GIL Readiness Failure
notes.body: Probe parameters are initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, successThreshold, failureThreshold — and mis-tuning them causes more outages than missing probes. Worked example (real panel scenario): a single-threaded Python web app keeps failing readiness under load. Diagnosis: the GIL means one thread handles requests AND the /ready endpoint; under load, request handling starves the probe endpoint, timeouts pile up, the pod is pulled from Endpoints, traffic shifts to remaining pods, they overload in turn — cascading failure. Solution: separate the probe from the request path (dedicated lightweight /readyz that doesn't queue behind app work, or a threaded/async server), set timeoutSeconds generously but periodSeconds tight enough to detect real death, and use startup probes for slow boots instead of huge initialDelays. Cloud-native guidance for services that 'fall over under load failing health checks': async/non-blocking handlers, separate probe endpoints, and timeouts everywhere — so health checking measures the app, not the queue.

cards.front: What does a CPU/memory REQUEST control? What does a LIMIT control?
cards.back: Request: scheduling placement (scheduler reserves it). Limit: kernel enforcement (max the container may use).

cards.front: CPU is compressible, memory is incompressible. What happens when each exceeds its limit?
cards.back: CPU: throttled (slowed, not killed). Memory: the kernel OOM-kills the process (exit 137).

cards.front: What is a millicore? How many millicores in 2.5 CPUs?
cards.back: 1/1000 of a CPU core. 2.5 CPU = 2500m.

cards.front: Node has 4000m CPU free; pods request 500m each. How many schedule (ignoring memory)?
cards.back: 8 (4000/500). The scheduler bin-packs on the tighter of the CPU and memory constraints.

cards.front: nginx pod: requests {16Gi, 0.5cpu}, limits {32Gi, 8cpu}. Name two production problems.
cards.back: 16Gi memory request starves the cluster (scheduling failures for others); 8-CPU limit lets one pod burst and throttle neighbors (noisy neighbor). Right-size both.

cards.front: App needs 2Gi minimum to start; request is 1Gi, limit 1Gi. What happens?
cards.back: It schedules (scheduler sees only the 1Gi request), then OOMKills during startup — CrashLoopBackOff, exit 137.

cards.front: Decode exit code 137 and name its usual Kubernetes reason.
cards.back: 128 + 9 = SIGKILL. Usual reason: OOMKilled — the container exceeded its memory limit.

cards.front: Where in kubectl describe pod do you confirm OOMKilled?
cards.back: The container's lastState: Terminated with Reason: OOMKilled and Exit Code: 137.

cards.front: State the job of each probe: startup, readiness, liveness.
cards.back: Startup: 'finished initializing?' (gates the other probes). Readiness: 'ready for traffic?' (failure removes from Endpoints, no restart). Liveness: 'still alive?' (failure restarts the container).

cards.front: A running pod suddenly restarts with no deploy. Which probe failed?
cards.back: Liveness — it's the only probe that restarts a running container.

cards.front: Why does a single-threaded Python app fail readiness under load (GIL)?
cards.back: One thread serves requests and the probe endpoint; under load the probe starves, times out, and the pod is wrongly pulled from Endpoints — cascading to other pods.

cards.front: Fix for GIL-starved readiness probes?
cards.back: Separate lightweight probe endpoint off the request path (or threaded/async server), plus sane timeouts; use startup probes for slow boots.

quiz.q: A container has requests {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi} and limits {cpu: 1000m, memory: 512Mi}. Which statement is TRUE?
choices: The scheduler reserves 1000m CPU for this container
The container is guaranteed 200m CPU for scheduling and will be OOM-killed above 512Mi memory
The container can never use more than 200m CPU
Memory above 256Mi is throttled like CPU
quiz.explain: Requests drive scheduling (200m reserved); limits cap usage — CPU throttles at 1000m, memory kills at 512Mi. Memory is never throttled.

quiz.q: Panel YAML review: frontend pod requests memory 16Gi, cpu 0.5; limits memory 32Gi, cpu 8. What breaks later?
choices: Nothing — generous resources are always safe
The 16Gi request starves cluster memory causing Pending scheduling failures elsewhere; the 8-CPU limit risks noisy-neighbor throttling
The pod will be OOM-killed immediately
CPU request 0.5 is invalid — must be an integer
quiz.explain: Over-requesting memory is a cluster-wide hazard (scheduler reserves it), and a huge CPU limit lets one pod burst over neighbors. Right-size from measured usage.

quiz.q: nginx needs minimum 2Gi to start; request is 1Gi, limit unset. It schedules. What happens under node memory pressure?
choices: It is protected because it scheduled successfully
It is among the first evicted — it exceeds its request, making it a Burstable eviction candidate
The scheduler moves it to another node live
CPU throttling keeps it alive
quiz.explain: Exceeding requests doesn't kill immediately without a limit, but the kubelet evicts over-request pods first under node pressure. Honest requests prevent this.

quiz.q: Container svc-basic terminated with exit code 137. Your diagnosis?
choices: Application panic — read the traceback
OOMKilled — the container exceeded its memory limit; confirm in lastState and raise the limit or cut memory use
Node disk full — free disk space
Image pull failure — check the tag
quiz.explain: 137 = SIGKILL; in Kubernetes this is the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit. describe pod's lastState confirms Reason: OOMKilled.

quiz.q: A pod runs fine for an hour, then the container restarts with no deployment. Which probe is implicated?
choices: Readiness — it restarts unhealthy pods
Liveness — it's the only probe that restarts a running container
Startup — it re-runs hourly
None — probes never restart containers
quiz.explain: Readiness only removes from Endpoints; startup only gates initialization. A mid-life restart is liveness (or an OOM kill — check lastState to distinguish).

quiz.q: Your liveness probe hits the same /api/search endpoint users hit. Under load the pod restart-loops. Best fix?
choices: Increase the CPU limit
Point liveness at a cheap /healthz endpoint that proves the process is alive, and keep deep checks in readiness
Delete the liveness probe
Set failureThreshold to 100
quiz.explain: Liveness should test 'alive', cheaply — an expensive endpoint makes the probe measure load, not life, and restarts cascade. Deep dependency checks belong in readiness.

quiz.q: A Java app takes 90s to warm up and keeps getting liveness-killed at 60s. Correct fix?
choices: Raise the CPU request
Add a startup probe with a generous failureThreshold covering warmup, so liveness/readiness stay disabled until boot completes
Set initialDelaySeconds: 600 on liveness
Remove all probes
quiz.explain: Startup probes exist for exactly this: they gate the other probes during initialization. A giant initialDelay is brittle — startup probes adapt to actual boot time.

quiz.q: Single-threaded Python app fails readiness under load due to the GIL. What is the structural fix?
choices: More CPU limit
Serve the probe on a separate lightweight path/thread (or use an async/threaded server) so health checks don't queue behind app work
Longer periodSeconds
Bigger memory request
quiz.explain: The probe must not compete with request handling on the single thread. Isolate it; tune timeouts second. Resources don't fix starvation of the probe endpoint.

quiz.q: kubectl top shows a pod using 480Mi with a 512Mi limit and frequent 137 restarts at peak. Two valid fixes?
choices: Raise the limit to cover the peak working set, or reduce the app's memory footprint (fix leak / bound caches)
Add CPU and delete the pod
Lower the request to 128Mi
Move the pod to a bigger node
quiz.explain: The working set genuinely exceeds the limit at peak — either the limit must reflect reality or the footprint must shrink. Changing requests or nodes doesn't change the cgroup cap.

items.prompt: Node: 8 CPU / 32Gi free. Pods request 1000m / 4Gi, limit 2000m / 8Gi. How many schedule?
items.answer: 8 — by both CPU (8000/1000) and memory (32/4). Both dimensions bind at 8.
items.explain: Compute per-dimension capacity and take the minimum; limits don't affect scheduling, only requests do.

items.prompt: Same node, pods now request 500m / 8Gi. How many schedule, and what limits them?
items.answer: 4 — memory binds (32/8 = 4) while CPU would allow 16.
items.explain: Always name the binding dimension; it trains you to see which resource to add or which request to trim.

items.prompt: A pod requests 100m CPU with no limit on a 4-CPU node shared with 3 identical pods, all idle except one that spikes. What happens to the spiking pod?
items.answer: It bursts freely up to available CPU — no limit means no throttle; the 100m request only guaranteed its scheduling slot.
items.explain: No limit = unbounded burst. That's why production namespaces set LimitRanges/default limits.

items.prompt: Pod A requests 3Gi, limit 3Gi; Pod B requests 1Gi, no limit; node hits memory pressure. Who gets evicted first?
items.answer: Pod B — it exceeds its request (Burstable), while Pod A is Guaranteed (request == limit) and evicted last.
items.explain: QoS classes: Guaranteed (request==limit for all containers) evicted last; Burstable exceeding requests evicted first.

items.prompt: You set requests {cpu: 2, memory: 4Gi} 'to be safe' for an app using 100m/256Mi. Name the cluster-level harm.
items.answer: You reserve 20x CPU and 16x memory the app never uses — the scheduler sees a full cluster while nodes sit idle, causing Pending for real workloads.
items.explain: Over-requesting is the most common self-inflicted capacity crisis; requests must track measured usage.

items.prompt: Container limit 1Gi, app's steady state is 900Mi, startup spike is 1.2Gi. Predict behavior.
items.answer: OOMKilled during startup (spike exceeds limit) → CrashLoopBackOff 137, even though steady state would fit.
items.explain: Limits apply at every instant, including startup spikes. Size limits for peak, not average.

items.prompt: Two containers in one pod: c1 requests 500m/512Mi, c2 requests 500m/512Mi. What does the SCHEDULER see for the pod?
items.answer: The sum: 1000m CPU / 1Gi memory — pod-level scheduling uses the total of container requests.
items.explain: Requests and limits are per-container but scheduling sums them per pod; a sidecar's requests count against placement too.

items.prompt: LimitRange sets default request 100m/128Mi. A manifest specifies only limits {500m, 512Mi}. Effective request?
items.answer: 100m/128Mi from the LimitRange default — the pod schedules as if it requested those.
items.explain: Unspecified requests fall back to LimitRange defaults; always check what the namespace injects.

items.prompt: Pod Running, restartCount 0, but kubectl get endpoints shows no addresses. Which probe failed and what did it do?
items.answer: Readiness failed — the pod was removed from Endpoints without being restarted.
items.explain: Zero restarts + no endpoints = readiness, the signature pattern. Check the readiness probe definition and the app's /ready output.

items.prompt: Pod restartCount climbs every ~2 minutes; events show 'Liveness probe failed: connection refused'. App logs show normal startup. Likely cause?
items.answer: The liveness probe hits the app before it's ready (no startup probe / too-small initialDelay) or probes the wrong port/path.
items.explain: Connection refused on liveness with healthy logs = probe misconfiguration, not app failure. Add a startup probe or fix the probe target.

items.prompt: You add a liveness probe with periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3 to a slow API. What is the maximum detection-to-restart time?
items.answer: ~15s of consecutive failures (plus the initial delay) — 3 failed periods × 5s.
items.explain: failureThreshold × periodSeconds bounds detection time; tune it against your tolerance for false positives vs. dead-pod time.

items.prompt: Readiness probe execs a script that checks the database. DB goes down for 30s. Describe the blast radius with correct probes.
items.answer: Pods fail readiness, leave Endpoints, traffic drains; when the DB recovers, probes pass and pods rejoin — no restarts, no cascade.
items.explain: This is readiness done right: dependency failures shed traffic instead of killing containers.

items.prompt: Same DB outage, but the check is in the LIVENESS probe. What happens?
items.answer: Every pod restarts, likely simultaneously — restart storm; slow-starting apps may never rejoin, cascading the outage.
items.explain: Never put dependency checks in liveness: a downstream blip becomes a self-inflicted mass restart.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Pod runs, then suddenly restarts — which probe?' Answer in one sentence with the reasoning.
items.answer: Liveness — it's the only probe whose failure restarts a running container; I'd confirm via the event and rule out OOMKilled in lastState.
items.explain: Name the probe, state the mechanism, and show you distinguish it from 137 — the complete panel answer.

items.prompt: Your probe: httpGet /healthz, timeoutSeconds: 1, on an app whose p99 latency is 800ms. Symptom and fix?
items.answer: Flapping readiness/liveness from timeouts near p99; raise timeoutSeconds (e.g. 5) so the probe tolerates normal latency.
items.explain: Timeouts must clear the app's normal latency with margin, or the probe measures tail latency instead of health.

items.prompt: Why must the liveness endpoint be cheap and side-effect free?
items.answer: It runs for the life of the pod at every period — an expensive or mutating check adds load and can itself cause the failures it detects.
items.explain: Probes are overhead you pay forever; keep liveness trivial ('process alive'), put depth in readiness.

handsOnLab.title: Break It With Resources, Fix It With Probes
handsOnLab.brief: Deploy workloads with deliberate resource misconfigurations, trigger a real OOMKilled, diagnose it from lastState, then add and tune all three probes on a slow-starting app.
steps: Create namespace res-lab; deploy a memory-hungry app with requests {128Mi} and limits {128Mi}.
Drive memory past the limit; observe CrashLoopBackOff and capture the OOMKilled/137 evidence from describe.
Raise the limit to fit the real working set; verify restarts stop and record the before/after values.
Deploy the panel's nginx spec (requests 16Gi/0.5, limits 32Gi/8) on your cluster; observe the scheduling impact and document it.
Right-size the nginx spec from measured usage (kubectl top) and re-deploy; compare node allocation.
Deploy a slow-starting app (sleep 60 in init) with only a liveness probe; watch it get killed mid-boot.
Add a startup probe covering the boot window; verify the app now survives startup and liveness takes over.
Break the app's dependency (point it at a dead DB host); confirm readiness removes it from Endpoints with zero restarts.
Move the dependency check into liveness temporarily; observe the restart storm, then revert.
Write the probe decision table your team will use: which check goes in which probe, with timeout guidance.
handsOnLab.deliverable: OOMKilled evidence capture, right-sized nginx spec with justification, probe decision table, and before/after manifests.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can produce an OOMKilled on demand, read it from lastState, and explain why each probe lives where it does in your manifests.

mockTask.q: Panel: they show the frontend pod YAML — image nginx:v4, requests {memory: 16Gi, cpu: 0.5}, limits {memory: 32Gi, cpu: 8} — and ask 'this goes to production as-is; what issues will you see later?'
choices: None — generous requests and limits are best practice for production safety
The pod will be OOM-killed on startup because 16Gi is too small for nginx
The 16Gi memory request will starve the cluster and cause Pending scheduling failures for other workloads, and the 8-CPU limit lets this pod burst-throttle its neighbors
The 0.5 CPU request is invalid and the pod will never schedule
mockTask.explain: Name both failure modes: memory over-requesting is a scheduling hazard cluster-wide (the scheduler reserves what you ask), and an outsized CPU limit creates noisy-neighbor throttling. Then give the fix: right-size from measured usage (kubectl top / metrics) and enforce sane bounds with LimitRanges. Panels want the cluster-level thinking, not just 'it's wasteful.'

title: Scheduling: Taints, Tolerations, Labels & Node Pools
summary: How pods get placed on purpose: labels and selectors, taints vs tolerations vs affinity, node pools, the cluster autoscaler, and the full runbook for Pending pods and 'out of nodes' — including the panel's node-pool and taint questions.
objectives: Use labels, selectors, and nodeSelector to target workloads at the right nodes
Distinguish taints, tolerations, and affinity and choose the right one for a placement rule
Argue the multiple-node-pools vs one-giant-pool tradeoff as a panel answer
Explain the cluster autoscaler's scale-up/scale-down behavior and its limits
Work the Pending-due-to-resources and 'out of nodes' triage from scheduler events to cloud-side causes

notes.title: Labels, Selectors, nodeSelector
notes.body: Labels are key/value tags on objects; selectors match them; nodeSelector is the simplest placement rule ('only schedule on nodes with this label'). Worked example: nodes are labeled workload=general or workload=gpu. Your ML training pod sets nodeSelector: {workload: gpu}; the scheduler filters out every node lacking that label and bin-packs among the GPU nodes. A teammate's pod with no nodeSelector can still land on GPU nodes — nodeSelector is a one-way preference, not reservation. Solution when you need true reservation: pair the label with a taint (next note). Everyday uses of selectors: Services find pods via selector, Deployments manage ReplicaSets via selector, and kubectl -l app=payments filters. The discipline: label deliberately (app, tier, workload-type) because every scheduling, routing, and policy mechanism in Kubernetes keys off labels.

notes.title: Taint vs Toleration vs Affinity
notes.body: Taints repel: a tainted node refuses pods unless they tolerate it. Tolerations permit: a pod declares which taints it tolerates. Affinity attracts: rules pulling pods toward (or away from) nodes or other pods. Worked example: GPU nodes carry taint dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule. Your training pod adds toleration {key: dedicated, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule} AND nodeAffinity preferring workload=gpu — the toleration gets it PAST the bouncer, the affinity steers it to the right room. Effects matter: NoSchedule blocks new pods, PreferNoSchedule tries to avoid, NoExecute evicts existing pods that don't tolerate (used for node maintenance/problem nodes). The panel one-liner: 'taints say who CAN'T come, tolerations are the pod's permission slip, affinity says where I'd PREFER to go.' Common exam trap: a toleration alone doesn't attract the pod to the tainted node — without affinity it may still schedule elsewhere.

notes.title: Affinity: Required vs Preferred, Pod Affinity
notes.body: Node affinity comes in two strengths: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution (hard rule — schedule ONLY here) and preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution (soft — try, with weights 1-100). Pod affinity/anti-affinity spreads or co-locates pods relative to each other. Worked example: you want payment pods spread across zones for HA: podAntiAffinity, required, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, matching labels app=payments. With 3 pods and 2 zones, the third pod goes Pending — required anti-affinity can't be satisfied. Solution: use preferredDuringScheduling with weight 100 instead: the scheduler spreads when possible but still places the third pod. The 'IgnoredDuringExecution' suffix is honest — if a node loses its label after scheduling, running pods are NOT evicted (only the NoExecute taint effect evicts). Rule of thumb: required for compliance (data residency), preferred for resilience (zone spread).

notes.title: Panel: Multiple Node Pools vs One Giant Pool
notes.body: Panel question: 'What is the benefit of multiple node pools versus one giant pool?' Model answer, structured: 'Isolation — a noisy or crashing workload in one pool can't starve the others, and I can cordon/drain one pool for upgrades while the rest serve traffic. Right-sizing — pools can use different VM SKUs: cheap burstable nodes for batch, memory-optimized for caches, GPU nodes for ML, instead of paying the max SKU for everything. Scaling granularity — the autoscaler scales each pool independently, so a GPU queue spike doesn't spin up general nodes. Blast radius — upgrades, kubelet config, and node image changes roll per pool. And taints per pool give me hard workload separation, like PCI workloads pinned to their own pool.' Worked contrast: one giant pool of 50 identical nodes means your GPU job waits behind a web traffic spike for the same autoscaler, and one bad node image affects everything. The cost: slightly more management overhead and potential fragmentation — small pools can strand capacity.

notes.title: Cluster Autoscaler: What It Does and Doesn't Do
notes.body: The cluster autoscaler watches for Pending pods (scale up) and underutilized nodes (scale down), then calls the cloud API to add/remove nodes per node pool. Worked example: 10 new pods go Pending with 'Insufficient cpu'; the autoscaler checks the pool's max count (say 10, currently 6), provisions 2 more nodes, the pods schedule, and the event stream shows 'TriggeredScaleUp'. Scale-down is conservative: a node is only removed if its pods can move elsewhere, it's been underutilized past the threshold, and no PodDisruptionBudget or local-storage annotation blocks it — scale-down can take 10+ minutes by design. What it does NOT do: fix Pending caused by taints, affinity, or PVC binding (no node count solves those); scale instantly (node provisioning takes minutes); or override pool min/max and cloud quotas. When 'insufficient resources' persists after scale-up, the problem is upstream of the autoscaler.

notes.title: 'Out of Nodes' Triage: Scheduler to Cloud
notes.body: Pods Pending with 'Insufficient cpu/memory' after the autoscaler should have acted — work outward from the scheduler to the cloud. Worked runbook: 1) describe pod — confirm the event is resources, not taints/affinity. 2) Check the autoscaler: are pools at max nodes? (az aks nodepool show / kubectl get nodes per pool label). If at max, raise it: az aks nodepool scale --cluster-name X --name pool1 --node-count 8 — the manual fix the panel asks about. 3) If new nodes still don't appear: check autoscaler logs, then cloud-side — subscription quotas, region/zone VM capacity, VM SKU restrictions, subnet IP exhaustion (each pod consumes IPs; a /24 subnet caps ~250), Azure Policy denying the SKU, taints on the new nodes, service-principal permissions, and Azure Activity logs/Resource Health for provisioning failures. 4) Consider max-pods-per-node and PodDisruptionBudgets blocking scale-down of old nodes. Solution mindset: Pending is the scheduler telling the truth about constraints — your job is to find which constraint, at which layer, and clear it.

cards.front: What is a label, a selector, and nodeSelector?
cards.back: Label: key/value tag on an object. Selector: query matching labels (Services, Deployments, kubectl -l). nodeSelector: pod field restricting scheduling to nodes with matching labels.

cards.front: One-line distinction: taint vs toleration vs affinity.
cards.back: Taint: node repels pods. Toleration: pod's permission to schedule on tainted nodes. Affinity: pod's preference/requirement toward nodes or other pods.

cards.front: What are the three taint effects?
cards.back: NoSchedule (blocks new pods), PreferNoSchedule (tries to avoid), NoExecute (evicts existing non-tolerating pods).

cards.front: A pod tolerates a GPU taint but schedules on a general node. Why, and what's missing?
cards.back: Toleration only permits — it doesn't attract. Missing: nodeAffinity/nodeSelector steering it to GPU nodes.

cards.front: Required vs preferred affinity — when would you use each?
cards.back: Required: hard compliance rules (data residency, GPU-only). Preferred (weighted): resilience goals like zone spread that shouldn't strand pods Pending.

cards.front: Give two benefits of multiple node pools over one giant pool.
cards.back: Isolation/blast radius (upgrades, noisy neighbors per pool) and right-sizing (different VM SKUs per workload instead of one max SKU).

cards.front: What triggers cluster autoscaler scale-UP? Scale-DOWN?
cards.back: Up: Pending pods that would fit on a new node. Down: underutilized nodes whose pods can relocate, respecting PDBs and cooldowns.

cards.front: Autoscaler won't fix which three Pending causes?
cards.back: Taints without tolerations, unsatisfiable affinity, unbound PVCs — no node count resolves these.

cards.front: Pods Pending 'Insufficient cpu', pool is at max nodes. What is the manual fix?
cards.back: Raise the pool max: az aks nodepool scale (or update) --node-count <n> — then verify nodes actually provision.

cards.front: New nodes still don't appear after scaling up. Name three cloud-side causes.
cards.back: Subscription/region quotas, subnet IP exhaustion, VM SKU restrictions, Azure Policy denials, SP permission failures, zone capacity (any three).

cards.front: Why might a /24 subnet cap your cluster's growth?
cards.back: Each node and pod consumes IPs from the subnet; ~250 usable IPs bounds total nodes × pods-per-node.

cards.front: max-pods-per-node matters for capacity planning because…
cards.back: A node with free CPU/memory can still reject pods once its pod-count cap is hit — IP and kubelet limits bind before compute does.

quiz.q: GPU nodes have taint dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule. Your ML pod has the matching toleration but no affinity. Where can it schedule?
choices: Only on GPU nodes
On any node, including non-GPU nodes — toleration permits but doesn't attract
Nowhere — tolerations require affinity
Only on the control plane
quiz.explain: Toleration is a permission slip, not a steering wheel. Without nodeAffinity/nodeSelector the scheduler may place it on general nodes, wasting the GPU reservation.

quiz.q: You apply NoExecute taint maintenance=true:NoExecute to a node. What happens to running pods without that toleration?
choices: Nothing — taints only affect new pods
They are evicted from the node
They are paused in place
They are moved to the control plane
quiz.explain: NoExecute is the evicting effect — the standard mechanism for node maintenance/drain. NoSchedule would only block new placements.

quiz.q: Panel: benefit of multiple node pools vs one giant pool. Strongest answer?
choices: Fewer YAML files to manage
Isolation, per-workload VM SKUs, independent autoscaling, and smaller upgrade blast radius
Pods schedule faster on one pool
One pool is always cheaper
quiz.explain: The panel wants the operational argument: isolation, right-sized SKUs (no paying GPU prices for web pods), independent scaling, blast radius. Acknowledge the fragmentation tradeoff.

quiz.q: Pods Pending 'Insufficient memory', autoscaler logs show the pool is at maxCount 5 with 5 nodes. Fix?
choices: Delete the Pending pods
Raise the pool max with az aks nodepool scale/update --node-count, then verify new nodes join
Add more taints
Increase pod memory requests
quiz.explain: The autoscaler is capped by maxCount — the manual fix is raising the ceiling. Then verify provisioning actually succeeds (quotas, IPs, SKU).

quiz.q: After raising max nodes, no new nodes appear. Azure Activity log shows 'OperationNotAllowed: quota exceeded'. What now?
choices: Keep raising max nodes
Request a subscription quota increase for the VM family/region, or use a different SKU/region
Delete the autoscaler
Set all pods to hostNetwork
quiz.explain: The cloud quota is the binding constraint — no Kubernetes setting overrides it. Raise the quota or change SKU/region.

quiz.q: Required podAntiAffinity across zones with 3 pods and 2 zones. What happens?
choices: All 3 spread evenly
The third pod stays Pending — required anti-affinity cannot be satisfied
The scheduler ignores the rule
One zone gets all 3
quiz.explain: Required means required: with only 2 zones, the third pod has no valid placement. Use preferredDuringScheduling for spread-without-stranding.

quiz.q: A node has free CPU/memory but rejects new pods. kubectl describe node shows 'pods: 110/110'. Cause?
choices: Taints
max-pods-per-node cap reached — IP/kubelet limits bind before compute
Insufficient CPU
Image pull failure
quiz.explain: The pod-count cap (default 110, often lower on Azure CNI) is a hard ceiling independent of compute headroom.

quiz.q: Scale-down never removes an old node at 10% utilization. What commonly blocks it?
choices: A PodDisruptionBudget that can't be satisfied, or pods with local storage
Too many labels on the node
The node is too old
Readiness probes
quiz.explain: The autoscaler won't evict if it would violate a PDB or strand local-storage pods — by design, scale-down is conservative.

quiz.q: Which Pending cause will the cluster autoscaler NEVER fix, no matter the max nodes?
choices: Insufficient cpu
Node taint that the pod doesn't tolerate
Insufficient memory
All Pending is fixable with more nodes
quiz.explain: Taints, affinity, and unbound PVCs are placement constraints, not capacity shortages — new nodes carry the same taints.

items.prompt: Nodes labeled tier=frontend and tier=backend. A cache pod must land on backend nodes only. Write the pod field.
items.answer: nodeSelector: {tier: backend}
items.explain: nodeSelector is the simplest hard placement rule — exact label match required on the node.

items.prompt: Same cluster: cache pods must ALSO never land on frontend nodes even if someone removes the backend label. Stronger construct?
items.answer: nodeAffinity requiredDuringScheduling with matchExpressions on tier=backend — still label-based; for true enforcement add a taint to frontend nodes.
items.explain: nodeSelector and affinity both trust labels; taints are the enforcement mechanism when labels might change.

items.prompt: You taint frontend nodes frontend-only=true:NoSchedule. Which pods need tolerations, and what breaks if you forget the backend pods?
items.answer: Only pods that must run on frontend nodes need the toleration. Backend pods are unaffected — taints only repel from the tainted nodes.
items.explain: Taints are node-local; forgetting a toleration only matters for pods that belong on the tainted nodes.

items.prompt: A statefulset needs its pods on distinct nodes. Which affinity, and required or preferred?
items.answer: podAntiAffinity on hostname topologyKey; preferred (weighted) unless distinct-nodes is a hard compliance requirement — required can strand pods Pending.
items.explain: topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname spreads across nodes; preferred avoids the Pending trap when nodes < replicas.

items.prompt: PCI workloads must run on dedicated nodes. Give the two-part construction.
items.answer: Taint the PCI nodes (pci=true:NoSchedule) + add the toleration to PCI pods + nodeAffinity steering them there; ideally a dedicated node pool.
items.explain: Taint enforces exclusivity, toleration grants access, affinity directs placement — the complete isolation pattern.

items.prompt: Pods Pending with 'didn't match Pod's node affinity' after a node relabel. Root cause?
items.answer: The nodes' labels changed (or were never applied); the pod's required affinity now matches zero nodes.
items.explain: Affinity trusts labels absolutely — relabeling nodes is a scheduling-affecting change, treat it like config.

items.prompt: You want canary pods (v2) to prefer the new node pool but still schedule on the old pool if the new one is full. Construct it.
items.answer: preferredDuringScheduling nodeAffinity with high weight toward the new pool's label — preference, not requirement.
items.explain: Preferred affinity expresses 'try here first' without stranding; required would Pending the canary when the new pool fills.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Why multiple node pools instead of one giant pool?' Give the 30-second answer.
items.answer: 'Isolation and blast radius, per-workload VM SKUs instead of one max SKU, independent autoscaling per pool, and per-pool taints for hard workload separation — at the cost of some capacity fragmentation.'
items.explain: Four benefits + one honest tradeoff = a complete panel answer. Deliver it as one flowing sentence.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Taint vs toleration vs label — go.' One breath.
items.answer: 'Labels describe, selectors match; taints repel pods from nodes, tolerations are the pod's permission to stay, affinity steers toward preferred nodes.'
items.explain: The panel wants the crisp distinction — especially that toleration permits but doesn't attract.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Pods are Pending, insufficient resources. Walk me through it.' First three steps?
items.answer: 'Confirm the scheduler event is resources not taints; check pool utilization vs max and autoscaler activity; if at max, raise it with az aks nodepool scale and verify nodes join.'
items.explain: Scheduler truth → autoscaler state → manual ceiling raise. Ordered, each step gated on the previous.

items.prompt: Panel: 'You raised max nodes and nothing provisioned. Now what?'
items.answer: 'I check autoscaler logs, then cloud-side: quotas, region/zone capacity, VM SKU restrictions, subnet IP exhaustion, Azure Policy, SP permissions, and Activity logs for the provisioning failure.'
items.explain: The full cloud-side checklist, delivered as the second half of the triage — shows you think past Kubernetes into the platform.

items.prompt: How do you manually increase max nodes per pool? Give the command shape.
items.answer: az aks nodepool scale --cluster-name <cluster> --name <pool> --node-count <n> (or az aks nodepool update --max-count).
items.explain: The panel asked this directly in the sessions — have the command shape memorized, not approximated.

items.prompt: Panel: 'A pod is Running on a node, then the node gets a NoExecute taint. What happens?'
items.answer: 'Pods without a matching toleration are evicted; the controllers reschedule them elsewhere. That's the standard drain/maintenance mechanism.'
items.explain: NoExecute is the evicting effect — this is how kubectl drain works under the hood.

items.prompt: Panel: 'When would you NOT use multiple node pools?'
items.answer: 'Tiny clusters where pool fragmentation strands capacity, or truly homogeneous workloads where one SKU fits everything — then the management overhead buys nothing.'
items.explain: Showing when NOT to use the pattern proves you understand the tradeoff, not just the slogan.

handsOnLab.title: Place Pods on Purpose
handsOnLab.brief: Label and taint nodes in a lab cluster, then place workloads with nodeSelector, tolerations, and affinity — including a dedicated 'PCI-like' pool — and simulate the Pending/out-of-nodes triage.
steps: Create a kind cluster with 3 workers; label one node workload=gpu and another tier=frontend.
Taint the gpu-labeled node dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule.
Deploy a pod with nodeSelector {workload: gpu} but no toleration; observe Pending and read the event.
Add the matching toleration; verify it schedules on the gpu node.
Deploy a general pod with no selectors; note where it lands and explain why the taint didn't stop it from landing elsewhere.
Add preferred podAntiAffinity (hostname topology) to a 3-replica Deployment; verify spread across nodes.
Change it to required anti-affinity and scale to 4 replicas; observe the 4th go Pending and explain.
Revert to preferred; simulate 'out of nodes' by setting an absurd memory request and work the triage: event → pool capacity → quota reasoning.
If on AKS: create a second node pool, taint it, and practice az aks nodepool scale up and down.
Document your team's labeling/tainting standard: which labels, which taints, which pool for which workload class.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Lab journal with each scenario's manifest snippet, scheduler event, and outcome — plus the written labeling/tainting standard.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can predict, before applying, exactly which node each pod will land on — and explain every Pending event in one sentence.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your team proposes one giant node pool of 60 identical nodes for everything — web, batch, and GPU training. Argue for or against.'
choices: For — one pool is simpler and simplicity always wins

Against — separate pools give isolation, right-sized SKUs per workload, independent autoscaling, and smaller blast radius; one pool forces GPU-priced nodes for web traffic and lets one workload starve the rest
Against — Kubernetes doesn't support pools larger than 10 nodes
For — taints don't work across multiple pools
mockTask.explain: Argue against with the four structural reasons (isolation, SKU right-sizing, independent autoscaling, blast radius) and name the real tradeoff (fragmentation/management overhead) to show balanced judgment. One pool means web pods compete with GPU jobs for the same autoscaler and you pay the max SKU everywhere.

videos.blurb: The official reference on taints, tolerations, and their effects — the exact semantics the panel questions in this module probe.

title: Services, Ingress & DNS
summary: How traffic finds pods and stays on healthy ones: Service types, Endpoints, kube-proxy, CoreDNS service discovery, Ingress routing, and where the Gateway API fits.
objectives: Choose between ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer and explain what each exposes
Diagnose 'Service has no endpoints' from selector mismatches and failing readiness
Explain how kube-proxy turns a Service into node-level forwarding rules
Use CoreDNS names for service discovery and avoid the ndots:5 trap
Write Ingress rules for host/path routing and describe what the Gateway API adds

notes.title: Service Types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer
notes.body: A Service is a stable virtual IP + DNS name in front of a set of pods selected by labels. ClusterIP (default): reachable only inside the cluster — the standard for internal service-to-service calls. NodePort: opens the same port on every node's IP (30000-32767) — useful for dev and bare metal, never for production ingress. LoadBalancer: provisions a cloud load balancer pointing at the nodes — the way to expose a service to the internet on managed Kubernetes. Worked example: you deploy the checkout API with type ClusterIP and the frontend calls http://checkout.shop:8080 — clean. Then someone 'fixes' external access by switching it to NodePort and giving customers node IPs: now every node exposes the port, there's no TLS termination, no host routing, and node replacements break bookmarks. Solution: ClusterIP for internal, Ingress (next notes) for HTTP external, LoadBalancer only when you genuinely need raw TCP/UDP from outside.

notes.title: 'Service Has No Endpoints': The Classic
notes.body: A Service without endpoints accepts connections into a black hole — kube-proxy has nowhere to send traffic. Worked example: kubectl get endpoints web shows <none>, and curl to the ClusterIP hangs. You check the Service selector: app: web, tier: frontend. You check the pods: labels app: web, tier: front-end. Solution: the selector doesn't match — tier: frontend vs tier: front-end. Fix the label or the selector and endpoints populate instantly. The second classic cause: labels match but every pod fails readiness — endpoints only include READY pods, so a bad readiness probe empties the list with zero restarts to alert you. Diagnostic order: kubectl get endpoints (confirm empty), compare Service selector vs pod labels (kubectl get pods --show-labels), then check readiness probe status. This is the single most common 'my service is down' root cause in every cluster.

notes.title: kube-proxy: The Invisible Load Balancer
notes.body: kube-proxy runs on every node and translates Service objects into forwarding rules (iptables or IPVS): packets to the ClusterIP are DNAT'd to a randomly chosen ready endpoint. Worked example: Service checkout has ClusterIP 10.0.5.20 and 3 ready pods. A frontend pod curls 10.0.5.20:8080 — the packet leaves the pod, hits the node's iptables rule installed by kube-proxy, gets rewritten to 10.244.1.7:8080 (one of the backends), and returns. No central proxy is in the path (in iptables mode) — it's distributed NAT. When a pod dies, the Endpoints controller removes it, kube-proxy updates rules on all nodes within seconds, and traffic stops going to the dead pod. Solution to 'how does the ClusterIP actually work?': it's a virtual IP that only exists as rules on every node — which is why you can't ping it from outside the cluster and why debugging means checking endpoints first, rules second.

notes.title: CoreDNS and Service Discovery
notes.body: CoreDNS answers DNS inside the cluster: my-svc.my-ns.svc.cluster.local resolves to the ClusterIP; within the same namespace, http://my-svc works. Worked example: from a debug pod you run nslookup checkout.shop and get 10.0.5.20 — service discovery with zero config. The trap: the default ndots:5 resolver setting means any name with fewer than 5 dots gets the cluster search domains appended FIRST — so curl http://api.example.com from a pod first tries api.example.com.shop.svc.cluster.local, waits for NXDOMAIN timeouts, and only then resolves externally, adding seconds of latency. Solution: use fully qualified names with a trailing dot (api.example.com.) for external calls in latency-sensitive paths, or tune ndots. Debugging DNS: kubectl exec into a pod and use nslookup/dig against the CoreDNS service IP; check CoreDNS pod logs for forwarding errors to upstream resolvers.

notes.title: Ingress: HTTP Routing Into the Cluster
notes.body: Ingress is the HTTP-aware front door: one entry point routing by host and path to ClusterIP Services, with TLS termination. Worked example: you need app.example.com/ → frontend Service and app.example.com/api → api Service, both TLS. The Ingress manifest: rules with host app.example.com, paths '/' → frontend:80 and '/api' → api:8080 (pathType: Prefix), plus a tls section referencing a TLS Secret. An ingress controller (nginx, Traefik, or cloud-native) watches Ingress objects and configures itself; you point DNS at the controller's LoadBalancer IP. Solution notes: Ingress needs an IngressClass (which controller serves it), path matching is prefix-vs-exact sensitive ('/api' Prefix also matches '/apix' — order rules carefully), and TLS Secrets must live in the same namespace as the Ingress. This is the production answer to 'how do users reach my app' — not NodePorts.

notes.title: Gateway API: The Next Generation
notes.body: The Gateway API (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, etc.) is the successor to Ingress, fixing its limitations with role-oriented design: infrastructure teams own the Gateway (listeners, TLS, addresses), app teams own HTTPRoutes (matching, backends) — no more one shared Ingress object everyone fights over. Worked example: platform team creates a Gateway 'prod' with an HTTPS listener on 443; your team creates an HTTPRoute binding to that Gateway routing /payments to the payments Service with a timeout and retry policy — you never touch the Gateway. Compared to Ingress: richer matching (headers, query params, methods), explicit policy attachment, and a standard status subresource showing whether your route was accepted. Concept to carry: Ingress is a single-role, annotation-driven API showing its age; Gateway API separates concerns so platform and app teams stop stepping on each other. Learn Ingress deeply (it's everywhere today), understand Gateway API's shape (it's where the ecosystem is going).

cards.front: When do you use ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer?
cards.back: ClusterIP: internal service-to-service (default). NodePort: dev/bare-metal node-port exposure. LoadBalancer: cloud LB for internet-facing TCP/UDP.

cards.front: kubectl get endpoints shows <none>. Name the two classic causes.
cards.back: Service selector doesn't match any pod labels; or pods match but all fail readiness (endpoints only include ready pods).

cards.front: How do you compare a Service's selector against pod labels?
cards.back: kubectl describe svc <name> (Selector line) vs kubectl get pods --show-labels — the key/values must match exactly.

cards.front: What does kube-proxy actually do on each node?
cards.back: Translates Service objects into iptables/IPVS forwarding rules so ClusterIPs DNAT to ready pod IPs — distributed, no central proxy in the path.

cards.front: What is the FQDN of service 'checkout' in namespace 'shop'?
cards.back: checkout.shop.svc.cluster.local (short form checkout.shop, or checkout within the same namespace).

cards.front: What is the ndots:5 trap?
cards.back: Names with <5 dots get cluster search domains tried first — external lookups like api.example.com suffer NXDOMAIN timeouts before resolving. Fix: trailing dot (api.example.com.).

cards.front: How do you debug DNS from inside the cluster?
cards.back: kubectl exec into a pod, run nslookup/dig; check CoreDNS pod logs for upstream forwarding errors.

cards.front: What does an Ingress do that a Service cannot?
cards.back: Host/path-based HTTP routing, TLS termination, and a single entry point for many services — via an ingress controller.

cards.front: An Ingress path '/api' (Prefix) also matches '/apix'. How do you avoid surprises?
cards.back: Order rules carefully, use Exact pathType where needed, and test routing — Prefix matching is greedy.

cards.front: Where must the TLS Secret live relative to the Ingress?
cards.back: In the same namespace as the Ingress object.

cards.front: Gateway API roles: who owns the Gateway vs the HTTPRoute?
cards.back: Platform/infra team owns Gateway (listeners, TLS, addresses); app teams own HTTPRoutes (matching, backends, policy).

cards.front: One advantage of Gateway API over Ingress?
cards.back: Richer matching (headers/methods/query), explicit policy attachment, role separation, and standard route-acceptance status (any one).

quiz.q: You need customers to reach your web app over HTTPS with host-based routing. Correct approach?
choices: NodePort on every node with node IPs in DNS
Ingress with host rules + TLS, served by an ingress controller behind a LoadBalancer
ClusterIP and tell customers the cluster IP
hostNetwork on all pods
quiz.explain: Ingress is the HTTP-aware front door: host/path routing + TLS termination in one object. NodePort exposes raw ports with no routing or TLS; ClusterIP isn't reachable externally.

quiz.q: kubectl get endpoints api returns <none>. Pods exist with correct labels. Next check?
choices: Node disk space
Whether the pods pass their readiness probes — only ready pods get endpoints
The etcd quorum
The image pull policy
quiz.explain: Labels matching but no endpoints = readiness failures. Endpoints = ready pods matching the selector; check probe status and fix the probe or the app.

quiz.q: A pod curls http://payments:8080 successfully. What resolved 'payments'?
choices: The node's /etc/hosts
CoreDNS, mapping payments.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local to the ClusterIP
kube-proxy's DNS cache
The cloud provider's DNS
quiz.explain: CoreDNS serves cluster.local zones; the short name expands via the pod's search domains to the FQDN, resolving to the Service's ClusterIP.

quiz.q: External API calls from pods take 5+ seconds to start. Internal calls are fast. Likely cause?
choices: CPU throttling
ndots:5 — external names try cluster search domains first, incurring NXDOMAIN timeouts
Too few CoreDNS replicas
MTU mismatch
quiz.explain: The classic ndots symptom: external names with few dots get cluster suffixes appended first. Fix with trailing-dot FQDNs or ndots tuning.

quiz.q: Ingress rule: host shop.example.com, path / (Prefix) → frontend:80; path /api (Prefix) → api:8080. Request to /apiv2/users goes where?
choices: frontend
api — /api Prefix matches /apiv2
404 from the controller
Round-robin between both
quiz.explain: Prefix /api matches any path starting with /api, including /apiv2. Use Exact pathType or order more-specific rules first, and test.

quiz.q: What does kube-proxy do when a backend pod dies?
choices: Restarts the pod
Updates node forwarding rules within seconds once Endpoints drops the pod — traffic stops going there
Deletes the Service
Pages the on-call
quiz.explain: The Endpoints controller removes the dead pod; kube-proxy reprograms iptables/IPVS on all nodes. Pod restart is kubelet's job, not kube-proxy's.

quiz.q: Two teams fight over one Ingress object's annotations. What is the Gateway API answer?
choices: More annotations
Split responsibilities: platform owns the Gateway, each team owns its HTTPRoutes bound to it
One Ingress per pod
Delete the ingress controller
quiz.explain: Role-oriented design is Gateway API's core fix for Ingress's shared-object fights: Gateway (infra) vs HTTPRoute (app team).

quiz.q: You need raw TCP (non-HTTP) exposed to the internet on managed Kubernetes. Which Service type?
choices: ClusterIP
NodePort with manual firewall rules
LoadBalancer — provisions a cloud LB for TCP/UDP
Headless service
quiz.explain: LoadBalancer is the managed path for non-HTTP internet exposure. Ingress only handles HTTP(S); headless services give direct pod DNS, not external access.

quiz.q: TLS termination for shop.example.com isn't working; the Ingress references secret shop-tls. First check?
choices: The Secret exists in the SAME namespace as the Ingress and contains valid tls.crt/tls.key
The nodes' certificates
The container registry
The pod's service account
quiz.explain: Cross-namespace secret references are not allowed for Ingress TLS — the most common cause is the secret living in the wrong namespace or being malformed.

items.prompt: Service selector is app: api; pods are labeled app: api, version: v2. Endpoints are empty and pods are ready. What's wrong?
items.answer: Nothing in the labels shown — check for a hidden mismatch (e.g. app: api vs app:api with different whitespace/case) via --show-labels; also verify the Service port matches the container's port.
items.explain: When labels look right, compare byte-for-byte and check the port mapping — targetPort must hit a port the container actually listens on.

items.prompt: Service port 80 → targetPort 8080. The container listens on 80. Symptom?
items.answer: Connections accepted then refused/hung — kube-proxy forwards to 8080 where nothing listens.
items.explain: Port mapping errors are silent at the Service level; verify with the container's actual listen port (netstat/ss inside the pod).

items.prompt: ClusterIP works from pods but you need it from your laptop for debugging. Fastest safe method?
items.answer: kubectl port-forward svc/<name> <local>:<port> — no Service type change, no exposure.
items.explain: port-forward is the debugging path; changing the Service type for debugging is how temporary exposure becomes permanent.

items.prompt: Two Services select the same pods. Is this allowed, and when is it useful?
items.answer: Yes — e.g. an internal ClusterIP and a metrics Service with different ports selecting the same app pods.
items.explain: Selectors are many-to-many; multiple Services commonly front the same pods on different ports (app vs metrics).

items.prompt: Headless service (clusterIP: None) for a StatefulSet. What does DNS return?
items.answer: The individual pod IPs (A records per pod: pod-0.svc…), not a virtual IP — clients get direct pod addresses.
items.explain: Headless = no kube-proxy load balancing; used when clients need stable per-pod identity (databases, Kafka).

items.prompt: Endpoints show 3 addresses but traffic only reaches 2 pods. Where do you look?
items.answer: The source node's kube-proxy iptables/IPVS rules for stale entries, and whether the third pod's readiness flaps (endpoints lag probe state by seconds).
items.explain: Check kube-proxy rules on the SOURCE node's iptables/IPVS for stale entries, and whether the third pod's readiness flaps (endpoints lag behind probe state by seconds).

items.prompt: After a deploy, half the traffic 502s for 60 seconds. Probes are fine. Likely mechanism?
items.answer: Old pods removed from Endpoints before connections drain, or the new pods' readiness passes before the app truly serves — tune terminationGracePeriod/deregistration delay and readiness depth.
items.explain: Rolling-update 502s are usually drain/readiness-timing issues: preStop hooks + termination grace let in-flight requests finish.

items.prompt: From pod in namespace shop, what are the three valid ways to address service 'api' in namespace billing?
items.answer: api.billing, api.billing.svc, api.billing.svc.cluster.local (all resolve to the ClusterIP).
items.explain: Search-domain expansion handles the short forms; the FQDN always works. Same-namespace pods can use just 'api'.

items.prompt: nslookup from a pod returns NXDOMAIN for a Service that exists. Two checks?
items.answer: Confirm the querying pod's namespace vs the Service's namespace (short names don't cross namespaces), and check CoreDNS pods are running (kubectl get pods -n kube-system).
items.explain: Cross-namespace short-name lookups are the #1 NXDOMAIN cause; dead CoreDNS is #2.

items.prompt: You hardcode a pod IP in another pod's config. Why will this break?
items.answer: Pod IPs are ephemeral — every restart/reschedule changes them. Use the Service DNS name, which is stable.
items.explain: The entire point of Services: stable virtual IP + DNS over ephemeral pod IPs.

items.prompt: CoreDNS logs show 'SERVFAIL' for external domains only. Cause?
items.answer: Upstream forwarder unreachable or blocked (egress network policy / firewall) — cluster.local still resolves, proving CoreDNS itself is healthy.
items.explain: Split the failure domain: internal OK + external failing = upstream path, not CoreDNS.

items.prompt: An app does 1000 DNS lookups/sec for an external API and p99 latency spikes. Two mitigations?
items.answer: Use trailing-dot FQDNs to skip ndots search expansion, and/or run a node-local DNS cache; reduce lookup frequency with connection reuse.
items.explain: Each lookup pays the search-domain walk; FQDN + caching attacks both the latency and the load.

items.prompt: Why can't you ping a ClusterIP from outside the cluster?
items.answer: The ClusterIP only exists as iptables/IPVS rules on cluster nodes — there's no route to it from outside.
items.explain: Virtual IPs are node-local fabric constructs; external access requires NodePort/LoadBalancer/Ingress.

items.prompt: Ingress controller pod is CrashLoopBackOff. What is the user-facing impact?
items.answer: Existing routes keep working (data plane is programmed), but no config updates apply — new Ingresses/routes won't take effect until it's healthy.
items.explain: Controllers are control-plane: their outage freezes config convergence, it doesn't instantly drop established forwarding.

handsOnLab.title: Wire Up Services, DNS, and Ingress
handsOnLab.brief: Deploy a two-tier app and expose it three ways; break service discovery on purpose (selector mismatch, ndots latency) and fix it; then front it with Ingress host/path routing and TLS.
steps: Create namespace svc-lab; deploy api (2 replicas) and web (1 replica) Deployments with distinct labels.
Create a ClusterIP Service for api; exec into web and curl http://api:8080 — confirm service discovery works.
Break the Service selector (change one label); confirm endpoints go empty and curl hangs; fix and verify recovery.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'The Service exists, pods are Running, but curl to the ClusterIP hangs. Walk me through it.'

'I'd check kubectl get endpoints first: empty means selector mismatch or failing readiness. Then I'd compare the Service selector to pod labels, verify readiness, and confirm the targetPort matches the container's listen port.'
'I'd delete and recreate the Service with a new ClusterIP.'
'I'd scale the Deployment to zero and back up.'

title: Helm: Charts, Values & Templating
summary: Package Kubernetes manifests the way professionals do: chart anatomy, values and templating, releases and revisions, install/upgrade/rollback — and the panel's 'why Helm instead of plain YAML' answered properly.
objectives: Describe chart anatomy (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates) and what a release and revision are
Render and debug templates with helm template, predicting output from values
Perform installs, upgrades, and rollbacks and read revision history
Argue 'why Helm instead of plain YAML' as a structured panel answer
Author an original chart for a multi-resource app following chart best practices

notes.title: Chart Anatomy: Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/
notes.body: A Helm chart is a directory: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, appVersion, dependencies), values.yaml (default configuration values), templates/ (Go-templated Kubernetes manifests), and optionally charts/ (bundled subcharts) and _helpers.tpl (named template definitions). Worked example: a chart named payments, version 1.3.0. values.yaml sets replicaCount: 2, image: {repository: payments, tag: v9}. templates/deployment.yaml contains replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} and image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}". Installing renders those placeholders into a real Deployment with replicas: 2 and image payments:v9. The key insight: the chart is the PACKAGE (versioned, shareable, pinned by version), values.yaml is the DEFAULT CONFIGURATION, and the release is the chart installed with specific values — one chart, many releases (dev, staging, prod) differing only in values. This separation is what lets a single reviewed artifact deploy safely to every environment without copying manifests.

notes.title: Values and Templating: Predicting Rendered Output
Releases, Revisions, and Rollback
notes.body: Installing a chart creates a RELEASE (a named instance: helm install payments ./payments-chart -n shop); every helm upgrade creates a new REVISION of that release, and Helm keeps the history. Worked example: release payments is at revision 3. You upgrade with a bad image tag — pods CrashLoopBackOff. helm history payments shows revisions 1-4 with statuses; helm rollback payments 3 reverts to revision 3's values and manifests, and the Deployment rolls back. Solution notes: rollback is fast because Helm stored every prior rendered manifest — but it rolls back VALUES too, so a config change bundled with the bad image also reverts (usually what you want). Guardrails: helm upgrade --atomic auto-rolls-back on failure, and --wait makes the command block until pods are ready instead of declaring victory at manifest-apply time. Revisions are your time machine — but only if you upgrade through Helm, never by hand-editing the live objects.

notes.title: Panel: Why Helm Instead of Plain YAML?
notes.body: Panel question: 'Why Helm instead of plain YAML?' Model answer, structured: 'Parameterization — one chart deploys to dev, staging, and prod with different values files instead of three copied YAML trees that drift. Versioning — charts are versioned packages, so I know exactly what 1.3.0 contains and can pin it. Lifecycle — install, upgrade, rollback, and uninstall are first-class operations with revision history; plain YAML has no rollback story. Reuse — one maintained chart (or a public one) serves every team instead of everyone hand-rolling Deployments. And hooks and tests — pre-install hooks for migrations, chart tests for smoke checks.' Worked contrast: the plain-YAML team keeps dev.yaml, staging.yaml, prod.yaml; a securityContext added to prod.yaml never reaches dev.yaml, and nobody can say which version is deployed where. Helm's values files make environment differences EXPLICIT and diffable — that's the operational win the panel wants named.

notes.title: Writing a Chart: Structure and Helpers
notes.body: Author charts like maintainers do. Worked example — chart for a two-tier app (api + postgres): Chart.yaml declares name: shop, version: 0.1.0, and a dependency on the bitnami/postgresql chart (helm dependency update fetches it into charts/). templates/ holds deployment.yaml, service.yaml, configmap.yaml for the api; _helpers.tpl defines named templates like shop.fullname and shop.labels used across every resource for consistent naming and labeling. values.yaml exposes ONLY what operators should change (replicaCount, image.tag, resources, ingress.host) — everything else stays in templates. The discipline: values.yaml is your chart's API — every value documented with a comment, sane defaults, required values validated with the required function ('required "db password needed" .Values.db.password') so misconfiguration fails at template time with a clear message, not as a CrashLoopBackOff at 2 AM.

notes.title: Safety: lint, template, dry-run, diff
notes.body: The chart safety pipeline catches errors before they reach the cluster. Worked example: you add a new value resources: {limits: {memory: 1Gi}} but indent it one space wrong in values.yaml — helm lint ./chart reports the schema issue; helm template --values prod.yaml ./chart renders and you spot replicas: <no value> where a typo'd .Values.replicacount returned nil (Go templates render missing values as '<no value>', not errors). helm install --dry-run=server goes further, validating against the real api-server without creating anything. Solution habit: lint → template → diff (helm diff upgrade, via plugin) → upgrade --atomic --wait. The panel-relevant story: 'I caught a nil image tag in helm template output during review — the pipeline would have deployed image :<no value> to prod.' Template-time verification is the cheapest verification there is.

cards.front: What are the three core parts of a chart, and what is a release?
cards.back: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (defaults), templates/ (templated manifests). A release is a chart installed with specific values — one chart, many releases.

cards.front: values.yaml sets replicaCount: 3; template has 'replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}'. Rendered output?
cards.back: replicas: 3

cards.front: What does the dash in {{- if }} do?
cards.back: Trims preceding whitespace/newline — controls blank lines in rendered YAML.

cards.front: Template references .Values.image.tag but values.yaml has no image key. What renders?
cards.back: <no value> — Go templates render missing values as '<no value>', not an error. Caught by helm template review.

cards.front: How do you preview rendered manifests without installing?
cards.back: helm template ./chart --values prod-values.yaml — renders locally; add --dry-run=server to validate against the api-server.

cards.front: Release payments is at revision 4 (broken). Command to revert to revision 3?
cards.back: helm rollback payments 3

cards.front: What does helm upgrade --atomic do?
cards.back: Automatically rolls back to the previous revision if the upgrade fails.

cards.front: Name three arguments for Helm over plain YAML.
cards.back: Parameterization across environments, versioned packages, and first-class install/upgrade/rollback with revision history (plus reuse, hooks, tests).

cards.front: What is _helpers.tpl for?
cards.back: Named template definitions (fullname, labels, selectors) reused across all resources for consistent naming/labeling.

cards.front: How do you force a clear error when a required value is missing?
cards.back: The required function: required "message" .Values.x — fails template rendering with your message.

cards.front: What does helm lint check?
cards.back: Chart structure and values/schema issues — the first static gate before template/install.

cards.front: Why should environment differences live in values files, not copied YAML trees?
cards.back: Differences become explicit, diffable, and reviewable — copied trees drift silently (the prod-only securityContext problem).

quiz.q: values.yaml: {replicaCount: 2, image: {repo: api, tag: v5}}. Template: 'replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}\nimage: {{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}'. Rendered?
choices: replicas: 2\nimage: api:v5
replicas: 3\nimage: api:latest
replicas: <no value>\nimage: <no value>
An error — nested values aren't allowed
quiz.explain: Straightforward value insertion: 2, api, v5. Nested maps are normal in values.yaml — the template path mirrors the structure.

quiz.q: values.yaml: {ports: [80, 443]}. Template: '{{- range .Values.ports }}\n- containerPort: {{ . }}\n{{- end }}'. Rendered?
choices: - containerPort: [80, 443]
- containerPort: 80\n- containerPort: 443
- containerPort: 80 only — range takes the first
Nothing — range needs a dict
quiz.explain: range iterates the list; '.' is each element in turn. Two iterations produce two list items.

quiz.q: values.yaml: {ingress: {enabled: false, host: x.example.com}}. Template: '{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}\nhost: {{ .Values.ingress.host }}\n{{- end }}'. Rendered?
choices: host: x.example.com
host: <no value>
Empty — the if block is skipped
An error — if requires else
quiz.explain: enabled is false so the entire if block (including the host line) is skipped. Conditionals cleanly include/exclude whole manifest sections.

quiz.q: An upgrade deployed a bad image tag; pods are crash-looping. Fastest recovery?
choices: helm rollback <release> <last-good-revision> — restores prior manifests and values
Delete the chart and reinstall from scratch
Edit the live Deployment by hand
Wait for the image to be fixed upstream
quiz.explain: Rollback is the first-class recovery: Helm stored every revision's rendered manifests. helm history identifies the last good revision.

quiz.q: Panel: 'Why Helm instead of plain YAML?' Best answer?
choices: Helm is newer
Parameterization per environment, versioned packages, and install/upgrade/rollback with revision history — environment differences become explicit values files instead of drifting YAML copies
YAML is deprecated
Helm replaces kubectl
quiz.explain: The three pillars — parameterization, versioning, lifecycle — plus the drift argument (copied trees diverge silently). That's the full-credit structure.

quiz.q: helm template output shows 'image: "payments:<no value>"'. What happened and what's the fix?
choices: The registry is down; retry
The template references a value missing from values.yaml — add the value or use required/default to fail loudly or fall back
The chart is corrupted; re-download
Helm version mismatch
quiz.explain: <no value> means the values path doesn't exist. Fix by defining it, defaulting it (default "v1" .Values.image.tag), or required-gating it.

quiz.q: You want dev, staging, prod from one chart. How?
choices: Copy the chart three times
One chart + three values files (values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml) selected with -f at install/upgrade
Three clusters can't share a chart
Edit templates per environment
quiz.explain: One chart, many value sets — the core Helm workflow. -f/--values overlays environment specifics onto shared defaults.

quiz.q: What does helm upgrade --wait change about the command?
choices: It skips the upgrade
It blocks until the workloads report ready instead of returning at manifest-apply time
It deletes old revisions
It upgrades Helm itself
quiz.explain: --wait makes the command honest: success means pods actually became ready, not just that manifests were accepted.

quiz.q: A chart needs postgres. Best practice for including it?
choices: Copy postgres YAML into templates/
Declare it as a dependency in Chart.yaml and run helm dependency update — versioned, maintained upstream
Tell operators to install postgres manually first
Run postgres as a sidecar
quiz.explain: Dependencies keep charts composable and versioned; vendored copies rot. Subchart values are configurable via the parent's values.yaml.

items.prompt: values: {name: web, replicas: 4}. Template: 'name: {{ .Values.name }}-svc\nreplicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}'. Render?
items.answer:
name: web-svc
replicas: 4
items.explain: Literal text concatenates with the inserted value: 'web' + '-svc'. Trace character by character.

items.answer: replicas: 5
items.explain: eq compares the strings; env is prod so the if-branch renders, else is skipped.

items.prompt: values: {hosts: [a.example.com, b.example.com]}. Template: '{{- range .Values.hosts }}\n- host: {{ . }}\n{{- end }}'. Render?
items.answer:
- host: a.example.com
- host: b.example.com
items.explain: range over the two-element list; '.' is each hostname in order.

items.prompt: values: {}. Template: 'tag: {{ .Values.image.tag | default "stable" }}'. Render?
items.answer: tag: stable
items.explain: Missing value is nil; the default pipeline substitutes 'stable'. Pipelines read left to right.

items.prompt: values: {tls: true}. Template: 'port: {{ if .Values.tls }}443{{ else }}80{{ end }}'. Render?
items.answer: port: 443
items.explain: Inline if/else without dashes; tls is true so 443 renders. (Dashes only affect whitespace.)

items.prompt: templates/service.yaml uses {{ include "shop.fullname" . }} and _helpers.tpl defines shop.fullname as '{{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}'. Release 'pay', chart 'shop'. Render?
items.answer: pay-shop
items.explain: include renders the named template with the current scope ('.' passed along); .Release.Name=pay, .Chart.Name=shop.

items.prompt: values: {resources: null}. Template: 'memory: {{ .Values.resources.limits.memory }}'. Render?
items.answer: Renders '<no value>' (or errors on strict nil dereference in some Helm versions) — never rely on it; guard with if/default/required.
items.explain: Chained access into null is the classic template crash. Defensive templates check existence first.

items.prompt: Install chart ./api as release 'orders' into namespace shop with prod values. Full command?
items.answer: helm install orders ./api -n shop -f values-prod.yaml (--create-namespace if needed).
items.explain: install RELEASE CHART; -n scopes the namespace; -f overlays values. Order of args matters: release name before chart path.

items.prompt: Upgrade release 'orders' to a new chart version with staging values, auto-rollback on failure, waiting for readiness.
items.answer: helm upgrade orders ./api -n shop -f values-staging.yaml --atomic --wait
items.explain: --atomic = rollback on failure; --wait = block until ready. The safe-upgrade incantation.

items.prompt: List releases in namespace shop and show revision history of 'orders'.
items.answer: helm list -n shop; helm history orders -n shop
items.explain: list shows releases; history shows revisions with status — the two commands that answer 'what is deployed where'.

items.prompt: Uninstall release 'orders' but keep its history. Then really remove everything.
items.answer: helm uninstall keeps history by default now (use --keep-history explicitly on older); full removal is helm uninstall orders -n shop (history purged per retention).
items.explain: Modern Helm retains release history on uninstall; know your version's behavior before promising auditability.

items.prompt: Your values-prod.yaml sets image.tag: v10 but the deploy shows v9. Two possible causes?
items.answer: Another -f file later in the command overrode it (--set or a later -f wins), or the release was upgraded without -f values-prod.yaml (fell back to chart defaults).
items.explain: Value precedence: --set > later -f > earlier -f > chart defaults. Always re-pass -f on upgrade.

items.prompt: helm upgrade fails with 'cannot re-use a name that is still in use'. Meaning?
items.answer: You're running install for an existing release name — use upgrade, not install.
items.explain: Release names are unique per namespace; install vs upgrade is the oldest Helm gotcha.

items.prompt: You hand-edited the live Deployment; next helm upgrade reverts your edit. Why, and what's the rule?
items.answer: Helm owns the rendered manifests — upgrade re-applies chart state, wiping manual edits. Rule: all changes go through values/chart + upgrade.
items.explain: Helm is the source of truth once adopted; out-of-band edits are silently reverted. Drift detection (helm diff) catches this.

handsOnLab.title: Author and Operate an Original Chart
handsOnLab.brief: Write a Helm chart from scratch for a two-tier sample app (API + database dependency), parameterize it per environment, and operate it through install, upgrade, failed upgrade, and rollback.
steps: Scaffold with helm create demo, then strip it to only what your app needs; study each generated file before deleting.
Write Chart.yaml (name, version, appVersion) and add a database subchart dependency; run helm dependency update.
Define _helpers.tpl with fullname and labels named templates; use them in every resource.
Write templates for Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap using values for replicas, image tag, and resources; document each value in values.yaml.
Add a required-gated DB password value; verify helm template fails clearly when it's unset.
Create values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml differing in replicas, resources, and ingress host.
helm lint, then helm template with each values file; diff the two renders and confirm only intended differences.
