mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your team manages 40 microservices with plain YAML — one folder per environment per service. Deployments are scary and nobody knows what's in prod. Pitch Helm.'
choices: 'Helm is the industry standard, so we should adopt it.'

'One versioned chart per service replaces 120 drifting YAML trees; values files make env differences explicit and diffable; upgrades get revision history and one-command rollback; and shared chart patterns (helpers, required values) stop every team hand-rolling Deployment boilerplate.'
'Helm deletes the need for kubectl.'
'Plain YAML can't do namespaces; Helm can.'
mockTask.explain: Pitch the concrete pains: drift (copied trees diverge), unknown prod state (no versioning/history), scary deploys (no rollback story), boilerplate sprawl. Then name Helm's answers to each. Panels promote the candidate who argues from operational pain, not fashion.

title: Terraform Fundamentals: Declarative IaC
summary: Infrastructure as Code the Terraform way: declarative vs imperative, providers and resources, the init/plan/apply loop, state as the source of truth, removing resources safely — and the panel's Terraform-vs-Ansible opener.
objectives: Contrast declarative and imperative infrastructure management and explain why idempotency matters
Read and write basic HCL: providers, resources, variables, and outputs
Run the init/plan/apply workflow and interpret a plan's create/update/destroy actions
Explain what state is, how drift happens, and how to reconcile it
Remove infrastructure via config removal vs the removed block, and argue Terraform vs Ansible as a panel answer

notes.title: Declarative vs Imperative: Say What, Not How
notes.body: Imperative says HOW: 'run these commands in order' (a shell script creating a VM: az vm create, then configure, then tag — run it twice and you get two VMs). Declarative says WHAT: 'a VM with these properties should exist' — Terraform compares desired state to actual state and only acts on the difference. Worked example: an HCL block declares azurerm_resource_group.main with name 'rg-shop-prod' and location 'East US'. First terraform apply creates it. Second terraform apply — with zero changes — reports 'No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.' Solution to 'why does this matter?': idempotency. The script is dangerous to re-run; the Terraform config is safe to re-run forever, which is what makes it reviewable in pull requests and runnable in pipelines. The panel one-liner: 'declarative describes the end state and converges; imperative describes steps and repeats them.'

notes.title: Providers, Resources, and HCL Blocks
notes.body: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) organizes config into blocks. terraform { required_providers } pins provider versions; provider 'azurerm' { features {} } configures authentication; resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main' { name, location } declares one real object — the block TYPE plus two LABELS (resource type, local name). Worked example: you need a storage account for the dev team. You write resource 'azurerm_storage_account' 'dev' with name 'stdevshop001', resource_group_name referencing azurerm_resource_group.main.name (a reference, not a copy — Terraform builds the dependency graph from it), account_tier 'Standard', account_replication_type 'LRS'. terraform init downloads the azurerm provider; terraform validate checks syntax. Solution insight: references create implicit dependencies — Terraform knows to create the resource group first because the storage account points at it. No ordering scripts needed; the graph does it.

notes.title: init / plan / apply: The Loop
notes.body: The workflow is always the same three steps. terraform init: downloads providers and configures the backend (one-time per working directory, re-run when providers change). terraform plan: refreshes state, diffs desired vs actual, and prints the action plan — '+' create, '~' update in place, '-' destroy, '-/+' replace. terraform apply: executes the plan after your confirmation. Worked example: you add the storage account block and run plan. Output shows: azurerm_storage_account.dev will be created (+), 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. You review the name, tier, replication — then apply. Solution discipline: plan is the code review for infrastructure — in pipelines, plan runs on every PR and apply only on merge to main, with the plan artifact attached. Never apply without reading the plan: a '-' you didn't expect is someone's production database.

notes.title: State: The Source of Truth (and Drift)
notes.body: terraform.tfstate maps your config to real-world IDs — it's how Terraform knows that azurerm_resource_group.main corresponds to the actual Azure resource. Worked example (real panel scenario): a teammate manually adds a data disk to the VM in the Azure portal. Next terraform plan shows NO changes — because the disk isn't in config OR state, Terraform is blind to it. Then someone runs apply after an unrelated change and... still no changes to the disk, but now your documented infrastructure lies. Solution: reconcile deliberately — either terraform import the disk into state (adopting it: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <resource-id>, noting the for_each address escaping with quotes) and add the matching config, or delete it manually to restore truth. The rule: state + config = documented reality; anything outside both is shadow infrastructure. Backends (azurerm, s3) with state locking exist so two applies never corrupt this file.

notes.title: Removing Resources: Destroy vs the removed Block
notes.body: Panel question: 'What exactly do you do in the Terraform file to remove a resource?' Two mechanisms, different meanings. Worked example: the dev storage account is no longer needed. Option A — delete the resource block from config, run plan: Terraform shows '- destroy' for the storage account; apply deletes the REAL Azure resource. Option B — replace the block with a removed { from = azurerm_storage_account.dev, lifecycle { destroy = false } } block: plan shows the resource dropped from state but NOT destroyed — the real storage account keeps running, unmanaged. Solution guidance: use plain removal when you want the infrastructure GONE (decommissioning); use the removed block when the resource must keep running but leave Terraform management (handing ownership to another team/tool). The panel wants the distinction named precisely: 'deleting the block destroys on apply; the removed block forgets without destroying.'

notes.title: Panel: The Biggest Difference — Terraform vs Ansible
notes.body: Panel question: 'What's the biggest difference between Terraform and Ansible? If Ansible can create VMs, why not just use Ansible?' Model answer: 'State. Terraform keeps a state file mapping config to real resources, so it knows what exists, detects drift, and plans minimal changes — create, update, or destroy exactly what's needed. Ansible is procedural and stateless: a playbook runs tasks in order with no memory of what it did before, so removing a VM means writing explicit removal tasks, and drift between runs is invisible. That's why you don't manage VM lifecycles in Ansible: no plan/apply safety net, no drift detection, painful ordering for dependencies.' Worked contrast: decommissioning 20 VMs in Terraform = delete the blocks, review the plan's 20 destroys, apply. In Ansible = write a teardown playbook and hope it matches what the build playbook created. Each tool's strength: Terraform for PROVISIONING lifecycle, Ansible for CONFIGURATION of what's already there.

cards.front: Declarative vs imperative in one sentence each.
cards.back: Declarative: describe the desired end state; the tool converges to it. Imperative: describe the steps; the tool repeats them.

cards.front: Why is Terraform's apply idempotent while a shell script isn't?
cards.back: Terraform diffs desired vs actual state and acts only on differences; re-running with no changes does nothing. A script re-executes every command.

cards.front: What are the two labels in resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main'?
cards.back: Resource TYPE (azurerm_resource_group) and local NAME (main) — the name used for references like azurerm_resource_group.main.name.

cards.front: What does terraform init do? terraform plan? terraform apply?
cards.back: init: downloads providers, configures backend. plan: diffs desired vs actual, prints + create / ~ update / - destroy. apply: executes the plan.

cards.front: In a plan, what do '+', '~', '-', '-/+' mean?
cards.back: Create, update in-place, destroy, destroy-then-recreate (replace).

cards.front: What is terraform.tfstate and why must it be locked?
cards.back: The map from config to real resource IDs — Terraform's memory. Locking (via backend) prevents concurrent applies corrupting it.

cards.front: A disk was added manually in the portal. Plan shows no changes. Why?
cards.back: It's in neither config nor state — Terraform is blind to it. That's drift; reconcile via import (+config) or manual deletion.

cards.front: Import address for a for_each managed disk instance 'disk1'?
cards.back: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <resource-id> — quote the address so the shell doesn't eat the brackets.

cards.front: You delete a resource block from config and apply. What happens to the real resource?
cards.back: Terraform plans '- destroy' and DELETES the real infrastructure on apply.

cards.front: What does the removed block do differently?
cards.back: Drops the resource from state WITHOUT destroying it — the real infrastructure keeps running, unmanaged by Terraform.

cards.front: Biggest Terraform vs Ansible difference, in one breath?
cards.back: State: Terraform tracks real resources, plans minimal changes, and detects drift; Ansible is stateless/procedural — no memory, no plan, drift invisible.

cards.front: If Ansible can create VMs, why not manage VM lifecycles with it?
cards.back: No state/drift detection, no plan/apply safety review, and teardown requires hand-written removal tasks that can diverge from build tasks.

quiz.q: You run terraform apply twice in a row with no config changes. What does the second run do?
choices: Creates duplicate resources
Reports no changes — the diff of desired vs actual is empty
Deletes everything and recreates it
Fails because state is locked
quiz.explain: Idempotency via state: the second apply diffs config against state+reality, finds no differences, and changes nothing. That's the declarative contract.

quiz.q: Plan output shows '-/+ azurerm_virtual_machine.web'. What will apply do?
choices: Update it in place with no downtime
Destroy and recreate it — expect replacement (and plan for the downtime/data implications)
Only destroy it
Skip it — -/+ means no-op
quiz.explain: -/+ is replace: some arguments force replacement. Treat it as a new resource — data disks, IPs, and downtime need explicit handling.

quiz.q: A teammate added a data disk to the VM in the Azure portal. The team must KEEP it. Correct reconciliation?
choices: Delete it — manual changes are forbidden
terraform import the disk into state (with the for_each-escaped address) and add the matching config, so plan goes clean
Ignore it — plan shows no changes anyway
Delete the state file and re-apply
quiz.explain: The panel's drift scenario: import adopts the real resource into state, then config codifies it — desired, actual, and documented all agree again.

quiz.q: Panel: 'What exactly do you do in the Terraform file to remove a resource?'
choices: Run terraform destroy -target on the command line only
Delete the resource block → plan shows destroy → apply deletes the real resource; OR use a removed block to drop it from state without destroying
Comment it out — Terraform ignores comments
Rename the resource
quiz.explain: Two precise mechanisms: block deletion destroys on apply; the removed block forgets without destroying. Name both and when each applies.

quiz.q: When would you use the removed block instead of deleting the block?
choices: When you want the infrastructure destroyed faster
When the real resource must keep running but leave Terraform management (e.g. handing ownership to another team)
When the resource is already destroyed
Never — it's deprecated
quiz.explain: removed { from=..., lifecycle { destroy=false } } = forget, don't destroy. The decommissioning path is plain block deletion.

quiz.q: Panel: 'Biggest difference Terraform vs Ansible?'
choices: Terraform is newer
State: Terraform tracks real resources and plans/detects drift; Ansible is stateless and procedural
Ansible can't touch cloud APIs
They're identical — it's just syntax
quiz.explain: State is the structural difference — it gives you plan/apply review, drift detection, and lifecycle management. Everything else follows from it.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't VM provisioning live in Ansible playbooks?
choices: Ansible is too slow
No state means no drift detection, no plan safety net, and teardown playbooks diverge from build playbooks
Ansible can't create VMs at all
Licensing costs
quiz.explain: Ansible CAN create VMs (modules exist) — the argument is lifecycle: stateless tooling can't manage lifecycles safely. Provision with Terraform, configure with Ansible.

quiz.q: Two engineers run apply simultaneously without a locked backend. Risk?
choices: None — Terraform merges automatically
State corruption: both write terraform.tfstate, one overwrites the other, and reality diverges from state
Double billing only
Plan becomes slower
quiz.explain: State is a single file both processes read-modify-write; without locking (azurerm/s3 backends provide it), concurrent applies corrupt it.

quiz.q: Where do provider credentials/secrets belong in a Terraform workflow?
choices: Hardcoded in provider blocks committed to git
Environment variables or a secret manager (e.g. Vault), injected at runtime — never in tfvars committed to git
In the state file — it's encrypted by default
Emailed to the team
quiz.explain: The session's real-world pattern: code on GitHub, secrets via env vars, tfvars excluded from git, Jenkins credential injection / Vault. State files can contain secrets — protect the backend too.

items.prompt: resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main' { name = 'rg-x' location = 'East US' } — what real object does this declare, and what is 'main'?
items.answer: One Azure resource group named rg-x in East US. 'main' is the local name for references (azurerm_resource_group.main.id).
items.explain: Type + local name + arguments. The local name never appears in Azure — only in your config's references.

items.prompt: resource 'azurerm_storage_account' 'dev' { resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name } — what does the reference do?
items.answer: Pulls the RG's actual name AND creates an implicit dependency — Terraform creates the RG before the storage account.
items.explain: References are both data flow and ordering. No depends_on needed when the graph is inferable.

items.prompt: variable 'location' { default = 'East US' } and the resource uses location = var.location. How do you override at apply time?
items.answer: terraform apply -var 'location=West US' (or a .tfvars file / TF_VAR_location env var).
items.explain: Variables are the parameterization seam; -var, tfvars, and TF_VAR_* env vars are the three override paths.

items.prompt: output 'rg_id' { value = azurerm_resource_group.main.id } — when is this useful?
items.answer: After apply it prints the real ID; other configs/modules consume outputs as inputs (composition).
items.explain: Outputs are a module's return values — the composition mechanism for multi-config setups.

items.prompt: terraform { required_providers { azurerm = { source = 'hashicorp/azurerm' version = '~> 3.0' } } } — what does this pin and why?
items.answer: The provider source and version constraint (~> 3.0 = >=3.0, <4.0). Pinning prevents a provider upgrade from silently changing behavior.
items.explain: Unpinned providers are a supply-chain risk: init could fetch a new major version with breaking changes.

items.prompt: Plan shows '+ azurerm_storage_account.dev' and '~ azurerm_resource_group.main'. In one sentence, what happens on apply?
items.answer: The storage account is created; the resource group is updated in place (e.g. tags changed).
items.explain: Read plans as sentences: + create, ~ modify, - destroy. Every apply should be narratable before confirmation.

items.prompt: You see count = 3 on a resource. What does Terraform create, and how are instances addressed?
items.answer: Three instances: azurerm_x.name[0], [1], [2]. (for_each uses string keys instead.)
items.explain: count = indexed instances; for_each = keyed instances. for_each is preferred when instances have identity (removing one doesn't shift the others).

drills.title: Panel Q&A: Terraform vs Ansible & Lifecycle

items.prompt: Panel: 'Biggest difference between Terraform and Ansible?' 30-second answer.
items.answer: 'State. Terraform records every real resource in state, so it plans minimal changes and detects drift. Ansible is procedural and stateless — it runs tasks with no memory, so removal and drift are manual.'
items.explain: Lead with the one word (state), then the two consequences (planning, drift). That's the full-credit shape.

items.prompt: Panel: 'If Ansible can create VMs, why not just use Ansible?'
items.answer: 'Because lifecycle needs state: decommissioning in Terraform is deleting blocks and reviewing a destroy plan; in Ansible it's a separate teardown playbook that rots. And drift — manual portal changes — is invisible to Ansible but shows in Terraform plan.'
items.explain: Two concrete costs: teardown divergence and invisible drift. Concrete beats abstract in panels.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Walk me through a resource's full lifecycle, testing to prod.'
items.answer: 'Write config in a branch, plan on PR, apply to dev, promote the same config through stage/QA with per-env tfvars, plan against prod, apply with approval — state per environment, same code.'
items.explain: The session's real workflow: GitHub code, env-separated state, plan-as-review, gated apply. Same config, different tfvars.

items.prompt: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account; here are the container names. Codify it.' What do you write?
items.answer: A resource group + azurerm_storage_account + azurerm_storage_container with for_each over the container names (later a map of name→access type when requirements change to per-container access).
items.explain: This is the session's for_each scenario: start with a set of names, evolve to a map when per-item config appears.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Requirements changed — each container needs its own access type (private/blob/container). Modify the code.'
items.answer: Change for_each from a set of names to a map of name→access_type, and set container_access_type = each.value.
items.explain: The canonical for_each evolution: set → map when per-instance attributes appear. each.key/each.value carry the data.

items.prompt: Panel: 'How was Terraform run at your previous job — where were secrets?'
items.answer: 'Code on GitHub, secrets via environment variables — tfvars never committed. Jenkins injected credentials at runtime, with Vault for secrets and Consul for config/service discovery.'
items.explain: The session's actual answer: code in git, secrets out of git, injected at runtime. Memorize this shape — panels ask it verbatim.

items.prompt: When is Ansible the RIGHT tool alongside Terraform?
items.answer: Configuration management on already-provisioned machines — installing packages, templating app configs, rolling service restarts. Terraform provisions; Ansible configures.
items.explain: The complementary framing: it's not Terraform-vs-Ansible as rivals, it's lifecycle vs configuration — each doing what it's designed for.

handsOnLab.title: Your First Terraform Lifecycle
handsOnLab.brief: Write HCL for a resource group and storage account, run the full init/plan/apply loop, evolve the config with for_each, simulate drift, and practice both resource-removal mechanisms.
steps: Install Terraform; write main.tf with terraform/provider blocks (azurerm, pinned version) and one resource group.
Run terraform init and terraform validate; explain what init downloaded and where.
Add azurerm_storage_account with a reference to the resource group's name; run plan and narrate every line.
Apply; confirm in the portal/CLI, then run apply again and confirm idempotent no-changes.
Add azurerm_storage_container with for_each over a set of three container names; plan and apply.
Evolve: change for_each to a map of name→access_type (private/blob/container); plan shows in-place updates; apply.
Simulate drift: manually change a tag in the portal; run plan and observe Terraform detect it; revert via apply.
Simulate unmanaged drift: manually add a second storage account in the portal; confirm plan is blind to it; import it with terraform import and codify it.
Remove one container from the for_each map; plan shows destroy for that instance only; apply.
Delete the storage account block; review the destroy plan; apply. Then practice the removed block on the resource group (forget, don't destroy).
handsOnLab.deliverable: main.tf evolution (git commits per step), plan transcripts for the drift and removal scenarios, and a one-page lifecycle cheat sheet.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can narrate any plan line-by-line, explain what state contains, and choose correctly between block deletion and the removed block.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your Ansible playbooks already create VMs. Convince me we need Terraform too.'
choices: 'We don't — Ansible covers everything.'

'Terraform's state gives us plan/apply review, drift detection, and declarative lifecycle: decommissioning is deleting blocks and reviewing destroys, while Ansible teardown playbooks diverge from build playbooks and manual portal changes stay invisible. Keep Ansible for configuring the machines Terraform provisions.'
'Terraform is faster at creating VMs.'
'Ansible can't create VMs, so we have no choice.'
mockTask.explain: Concede Ansible's strength (configuration), then land the lifecycle argument: state → plan review → drift detection → safe teardown. The winning frame is complementary, not replacement — 'Terraform provisions, Ansible configures' shows senior judgment, not tool tribalism.
